documents.title: IWGDF guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetic foot disease

chunks.content: Introduction Infected bone defects are common and serious complications following trauma, osteomyelitis, and revision surgeries, particularly when large bone defects of the limbs are accompanied by soft tissue damage [ ]. These bone defects often lead to recurrent infections due to the loss of mechanical support, persistent infection, and insufficient soft tissue coverage [ ]. Traditional treatments such as autologous bone grafting, the Masquelet technique, and Ilizarov bone transport face challenges such as long treatment cycles, a high incidence of complications (with infection recurrence rates ranging from 15% to 30%), and limited functional recovery [ – ]. In recent years, 3D-printed customized titanium alloy prostheses have provided a new direction for bone defect reconstruction after infection control, thanks to their advantages in precise anatomical matching, immediate mechanical stability, and microporous structure that promotes bone ingrowth [ , ]. The clinical application of 3D-printed microporous titanium in orthopedics initially began with the repair and reconstruction after bone tumor resection and limb-salvage surgeries, achieving favorable results [ ]. In osteomyelitis treatment, given the complexity and high cost of traditional Masquelet and Ilizarov bone transport techniques, personalized 3D printing technology can promote bone-prosthesis interface integration and bone ingrowth through porosity, while maintaining good mechanical support [ ]. Furthermore, soft tissue defects associated with complex cases remain a key factor limiting their effectiveness. The lack of well-vascularized soft tissue coverage significantly increases the risk of prosthesis exposure and recurrent infection [ ]. For the repair of soft tissue defects of varying degrees, free flap techniques (such as the anterolateral thigh free flap) can effectively reduce dead space, promote wound healing, and reduce the risk of deep infection by providing well-vascularized tissue coverage [ , ]. Current research on the treatment of infected bone defects primarily focuses on single treatment strategies, such as prosthesis implantation or local pedicled flap repair. For example, Liu et al. [ ] reported on the use of 3D-printed microporous titanium implants for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis, with 6 out of 8 patients achieving good bone integration. We also reported the use of single microporous titanium prosthesis implantation for treating 18 patients with infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis, with 17 patients (94.4%) achieving good healing [ ]. Previously, in 2022, we first reported the preliminary efficacy of free/local flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium for treating 6 cases of lower limb infected bone defects with soft tissue loss, with 5 patients achieving good wound healing (83.3%) [ ]. Additionally, Chen et al. [ ] used local transposition flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium to treat 13 patients with femoral bone defects following osteomyelitis, achieving good bone integration and wound healing in 7 cases during follow-up. However, the personalized harvesting of free flaps and the advantages of covering large soft tissue defects are not addressed in existing studies. On the other hand, current research is limited to lower limb cases, with a lack of evidence for the efficacy in upper limb infected bone defects. Importantly, these clinical efficacy and safety data have not been validated in large-scale studies. The biomechanical performance of the 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis has been systematically evaluated in our previous study using integrated biomechanical testing and finite element analysis, which demonstrated sufficient load-bearing capacity, favorable stress distribution, and resistance to fatigue failure [ ]. Building on this biomechanical foundation, we conducted the largest single-center retrospective cohort study to date to evaluate the clinical safety and effectiveness of a staged reconstructive strategy incorporating personalized 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses for infected bone defects. This strategy integrates individualized prosthesis implantation with free flap reconstruction when required, allowing its application to infected bone defects with varying degrees of soft tissue involvement at different anatomical locations in the limbs (Fig. ). In addition to assessing overall clinical outcomes, we explored risk factors associated with postoperative complications. Patients were further stratified into subgroups according to the presence or absence of significant soft tissue defects, namely a single prosthesis group and a combined free flap group. Rather than aiming to compare these subgroups for superiority, subgroup analyses were performed to characterize clinical features and recovery trajectories across different tiers of reconstructive complexity, thereby evaluating the applicability and universality of the staged treatment protocol. The staged approach consisted of: (1) infection control with or without individualized free flap coverage based on soft tissue requirements; and (2) definitive bone reconstruction using a customized 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis. Materials and methods Study design This is a retrospective study. Our institution specializes in the treatment of infected bone defects caused by various factors and has extensive experience in limb repair and reconstruction. After approval from the institutional ethics review board (2019-018-02), we conducted a retrospective data collection and analysis of a series of patients who underwent microporous titanium implant treatment from January 2019 to January 2025. This cohort study has been reported in line with the STROCSS guidelines [ , ]. Patient selection The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) For bone defect characteristics, patients with infected nonunion or traumatic bone defects in the limbs (including tibia, femur, humerus, radius, carpal bones, metacarpal bones, and metatarsal bones, etc.) where the bone defect length after debridement could not be repaired by traditional autologous or artificial bone grafts (confirmed by imaging measurements and 3D CT reconstruction); (2) Patients with concomitant soft tissue defects that could not be closed by direct suturing or skin grafting (evaluated by wound measurement software or intraoperative sterile film method); (3) Postoperative follow-up ≥ 3 months with complete imaging (X-ray/CT) and laboratory data. Additionally, the study excluded the following: (1) Severe uncontrolled underlying diseases (such as uncontrolled diabetes: HbA1c > 8%, heart failure grade III-IV, cirrhosis Child-Pugh class C) (2), Long-term use of immunosuppressants or corticosteroids (prednisone ≥ 10 mg/d, continuous use for > 3 months); (3) Tumor-related bone destruction (primary bone tumors or metastatic tumors), radiation-induced bone necrosis, congenital skeletal deformities; (4) Loss to follow-up or missing critical data (imaging, functional scores). All surgeries were performed by the same senior surgeon to reduce heterogeneity in the procedure. Surgical technique and postoperative rehabilitation This study employed a two-stage surgical approach to treat complex infected bone defects. Prior to the second surgery, a 3D CT scan was used to assess the morphology of the bone defect and the extent of soft tissue involvement, after which an individualized 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis was custom-designed (pore diameter 700–750 μm, porosity 65–75%). The first-stage surgery involved thorough debridement, removal of necrotic bone and soft tissue, and the implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement (2 g vancomycin/40 g bone cement). Simultaneously, a free anterolateral thigh flap was used to repair the concomitant soft tissue defect in 25 cases. Postoperatively, antibiotic treatment based on bacterial culture results was administered until the infection was completely controlled (CRP, ESR, and white blood cell counts normalized for two consecutive tests). In the second-stage surgery, the induced membrane was preserved, bone cement was removed, and the pre-designed microporous titanium prosthesis was implanted (secured by intramedullary protrusion anchor and titanium plate fixation). The surface of the prosthesis was coated with vancomycin sulfate calcium. Regardless of whether the procedure involved a single implantation or a combined free flap repair, all patients received standardized nursing and rehabilitation. Detailed information regarding staged surgery and postoperative rehabilitation can be found in Supplemental Material 1, including first-stage surgery, postoperative management, design and manufacturing of 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis, and second-stage surgery and postoperative rehabilitation. Data collection and outcome measures Outpatient follow-up and data collection were performed at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, with annual reviews thereafter. All follow-up data were collected and organized by research assistants, and electronic medical records were reviewed, including case files, surgical details, laboratory, and imaging data. The baseline data obtained for patients included age, gender, and medical history; primary characteristics included etiology (traumatic or non-traumatic) of the bone defect, location, length, soft tissue defect area, flap type, and bacterial culture results. Laboratory and imaging assessments (X-ray and CT) were performed preoperatively and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, with subsequent annual checks. Visual analogue scale (VAS) scores [ ] were recorded at each follow-up. CRP and ESR were measured at each follow-up time point, and infection control was considered achieved if the values normalized for two consecutive tests (CRP < 10 mg/L, ESR < 20 mm/h). Additionally, implant integration and stability were evaluated using X-ray and CT examinations. Successful implant integration was defined by fulfillment of all of the following criteria: (1) progressive trabecular bone formation at the bone–prosthesis interface; (2) absence of progressive radiolucent lines greater than 2 mm; and (3) absence of implant migration, loosening, or mechanical failure. Failure to meet any one of these criteria was classified as poor implant integration. For lower limb cases, postoperative functional recovery was assessed using the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS) [ ], recording the postoperative standing time, walking time with crutches, and time to full weight-bearing. Infection eradication was assessed based on a comprehensive evaluation combining clinical, laboratory, and radiological

Failure to meet any one of these criteria was classified as poor implant integration. For lower limb cases, postoperative functional recovery was assessed using the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS) [ ], recording the postoperative standing time, walking time with crutches, and time to full weight-bearing. Infection eradication was assessed based on a comprehensive evaluation combining clinical, laboratory, and radiological criteria. Clinical signs included the absence of sinus tract, persistent drainage, local erythema, swelling, or pain. Additionally, pre-defined complications included wound recurrent infection, flap necrosis, poor wound healing, prosthesis-related infections, prosthesis-related fractures, implant fractures, and non-union. Statistical analysis Data analysis was performed using IBM SPSS (version 29.0). For baseline data, continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) and categorical variables were expressed as frequency (percentage). Differences in LEFS and VAS scores before and after surgery were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Predefined complications (such as recurrent infection, prosthesis fracture, etc.) were treated as binary outcome variables. Univariate logistic regression was performed to assess the relationship between patients’ baseline characteristics (age, gender, bone defect length, etc.) and surgical features (flap repair, bacterial type, etc.). Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics From February 2019 to January 2025, 82 patients with osteomyelitis caused by trauma or non-trauma underwent staged surgeries. All patients signed an informed consent form for surgery. Two patients were excluded because they did not undergo the second-stage surgery after the first debridement and vancomycin-loaded implant. In the end, 80 patients met the eligibility criteria and were included in the analysis. Among these, 54 were male (67.5%) and 26 were female (32.5%), with an average age of 47.5 ± 9.3 years, an average BMI of 26.6 ± 2.9 kg/m², and an average follow-up time of 40.8 ± 14.8 months. The majority of infected bone defects were traumatic (52 cases, 65%). There were 24 patients with a history of hypertension, 10 with a history of diabetes, and 4 with both hypertension and diabetes. The median bone defect length was 11.4 cm (range 3.8–32.0 cm), and the soft tissue defect area ranged from approximately 5.0 × 8.0 cm to 33 × 10 cm (Table ). None of the 80 patients lost to follow-up at the last visit. Among the 55 cases in the single microporous titanium implant group, 37 were male (69.1%) and 18 were female (30.9%), with an average age of 47.0 ± 7.8 years and an average follow-up time of 42.8 ± 12.3 months. The range of soft tissue defect area was approximately 5.0 cm × 8.0 cm to 33 cm × 10 cm. The median bone defect length was 10.5 cm (range 3.5–28.0 cm), including 32 cases of tibial bone defects, 11 cases of femoral bone defects, 5 cases of humeral bone defects, 4 cases of radial bone defects, and 3 cases of combined carpal and metacarpal bone defects. In the free flap combined group, there were 25 cases, with 17 males (68.0%) and 8 females (32.0%), with an average age of 48.5 ± 12.1 years and an average follow-up time of 36.4 ± 15.5 months. The median bone defect length was 12.0 cm (range 3.8–32.0 cm), including 3 cases with extensive dorsal foot soft tissue defects accompanied by large segments of metatarsal bone defects, 19 cases with lower leg soft tissue defects accompanied by large segments of tibial bone defects, and 3 cases of hand and forearm soft tissue defects combined with metacarpal and carpal bone defects. The bacterial culture results from the first-stage surgery showed that among the 25 patients in the free flap combined group, Gram-positive (G⁺) infections accounted for 76% (19/25), primarily Staphylococcus aureus (14/25) and Staphylococcus epidermidis (5/25). Gram-negative (G⁻) infections accounted for 16% (4/25), all due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Mixed infections ( Staphylococcus aureus + Pseudomonas aeruginosa ) accounted for 8% (2/25). For the 55 cases in the single microporous titanium implant group, G⁺ infections accounted for 78.2% (43/55), with Staphylococcus aureus being the predominant pathogen (65.5%, 36/55), followed by coagulase-negative staphylococci ( Staphylococcus epidermidis in 7 cases). G⁻ infections accounted for 14.5% (8/55), including Pseudomonas aeruginosa (4/9) and Escherichia coli (4/9). Mixed infections accounted for 7.3% (4/55), with Staphylococcus aureus + Pseudomonas aeruginosa in 3 cases, and Staphylococcus aureus + Escherichia coli in 1 case. Overall clinical efficacy The average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.2 ± 1.4, which decreased to 1.6 ± 0.7 at 12 months postoperatively. The VAS score at the last follow-up was 1.2 ± 0.4 (Table ).

Overall clinical efficacy The average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.2 ± 1.4, which decreased to 1.6 ± 0.7 at 12 months postoperatively. The VAS score at the last follow-up was 1.2 ± 0.4 (Table ). At each postoperative follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up), VAS scores significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001). For lower limb cases ( N = 65), the average baseline LEFS score preoperatively was 28.5 ± 5.8, with significant improvements in the LEFS score at each follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up) ( p < 0.0001). The average time to first standing for lower limb patients was 2.1 ± 0.5 months, the average time to first walking with crutches was 3.8 ± 1.1 months, and the average time to full weight-bearing was 5.3 ± 0.9 months. Based on the implant integration by X-ray and CT examinations, the number of cases rated as “Excellent” and “Poor” were 69 (86.3%) and 11 (13.7%), respectively. The representative case is shown in Fig. . Subgroup analysis In the single microporous titanium implant group ( N = 55), the average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.0 ± 1.5. At each follow-up time point, VAS scores significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001; Fig. ). For lower limb cases ( N = 43), the average baseline LEFS score preoperatively was 29.2 ± 5.2, with significantly higher scores observed at each follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up) ( p < 0.0001). The average time to first standing for lower limb patients was 2.0 ± 0.6 months, the average time to first walking with crutches was 3.5 ± 1.1 months, and the average time to full weight-bearing was 5.1 ± 0.7 months. Based on the implant integration by X-ray and CT examinations, the number of cases rated as “Excellent” and “Poor” were 50 (90.9%) and 5 (9.1%), respectively. For the free flap combined group ( N = 25), the average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.6 ± 1.2. At each follow-up time point, VAS scores significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001; Fig. ). For lower limb cases ( N = 22), the average baseline LEFS score preoperatively was 27.1 ± 6.7, with significantly higher scores observed at each follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up) ( p < 0.0001). The average time to first standing for lower limb patients was 2.3 ± 0.5 months, the average time to first walking with crutches was 4.2 ± 1.2 months, and the average time to full weight-bearing was 5.8 ± 1.1 months. For implant integration, the number of cases rated as “Excellent” and “Poor” were 19 (76%) and 6 (24%), respectively. Complications A total of 8 complications occurred during the postoperative follow-up period among 80 patients, resulting in an overall complication rate of 10% (Table ). The complications were categorized as recurrent infections and prosthesis fractures, occurring at an average of 7.5 ± 3.6 months postoperatively. Among these, recurrent infection was the most common complication (7.5%), occurring at an average of 5.8 ± 3.1 months postoperatively. Prosthesis fracture occurred in 2.5% of cases, with an average onset at 11.5 months postoperatively. Notably, the tibia was the most common site of complications, accounting for 50% of all complications. Specifically, in the single 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis group, two patients experienced recurrent tibial infections at 6 and 11 months postoperatively. After debridement, vancomycin-loaded bone cement was implanted, and both patients resumed walking at 6- and 8-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent infection at 5 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 6 months post second-stage surgery. Another patient in the same group experienced a femoral prosthesis fracture at 13 months postoperatively, which was followed by prosthesis removal and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored 7 months after the second-stage surgery. In the free flap combined treatment group, two diabetic patients developed foot wound infections at 3 and 4 months postoperatively. Both patients underwent prosthesis removal and replacement with vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored at 5- and 7-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent tibial infection at 8 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 4 months after the second-stage surgery. In the free flap combined treatment group, two diabetic patients developed foot wound infections at 3 and 4 months postoperatively. Both patients underwent prosthesis removal and replacement with vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored at 5- and 7-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent tibial infection at 8 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 4 months after the second-stage surgery. Another patient had a tibial fixation prosthesis screw fracture at 10 months postoperatively. After revision surgery, walking was restored 5 months later, with no recurrence of infection observed. Risk factors of complications Exploratory risk factor analysis ( Table ) showed that diabetes mellitus was associated with a higher occurrence of postoperative complications in both univariate logistic regression (OR = 11; p = 0.004) and Fisher’s exact test ( p = 0.007). The increased risk of recurrent infection was associated with a history of diabetes (OR = 9.571; p = 0.013) and bacterial culture results showing mixed infection (OR = 8.75; p = 0.031). No significant associations were observed between other baseline characteristics and prosthesis-related mechanical failure. However, given the small number of events, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Discussion In this study, the most significant finding was that 90% of patients did not experience recurrence after receiving either single microporous titanium implantation or combined free flap treatment, with an average follow-up of 40.8 months. The postoperative 1-year VAS score significantly decreased from 7.2 ± 1.4 to 1.6 ± 0.7 ( p < 0.0001), and the LEFS score for the lower limbs increased from 28.5 ± 5.8 to a median score of 59.0 ( p < 0.0001). The implant integration was rated as “Excellent” in 86.3% of cases. Additionally, we found that a history of diabetes and mixed bacterial infections may be important risk factors for recurrent infections. Over the past few decades, both the Masquelet and Ilizarov techniques have been clinically applied as important treatment options for infected bone defects [ , ]. However, the effectiveness of these methods may be compromised by complications such as pin tract infections, donor site infections, non-union, mechanical issues, or even recurrent fractures [ , ]. Many patients are unable to bear weight during the early postoperative recovery period. For example, a previous clinical efficacy comparison analysis showed that the average fixation time for the Masquelet and Ilizarov groups was 10.15 months and 17.21 months, respectively, with the Masquelet group demonstrating better functional outcomes [ ]. For cases without soft tissue defects, our study showed a treatment success rate of 92.7% (51/55) in the single microporous titanium prosthesis implantation group, with complete weight-bearing achieved on average after 5.0 ± 0.7 months. Pain was significantly relieved at 3 months postoperatively and continued to improve until the last follow-up. This may be attributed to the protective role of complete soft tissue coverage on the prosthesis, preventing microbial colonization and mechanical stress concentration. For cases with soft tissue defects, despite more complex bone and soft tissue defects and reliance on microsurgical techniques for free flap coverage, a treatment success rate of 84.0% (21/25) was still achieved, which is consistent with previously reported success rates (82.3–96.5%) [ , ]. Postoperative pain and lower limb function continued to improve at 3 months and beyond, with full weight-bearing achieved at 5.8 ± 1.1 months. The core advantage of free flap combined reconstruction for infected bone defects with soft tissue loss lies in the vascular support provided by the free flap, which may further influence bone healing outcomes. Given the fundamental differences in baseline disease severity and soft tissue involvement between patients treated with single prosthesis implantation and those requiring combined free flap reconstruction, these subgroups were analyzed as distinct cohorts representing different tiers of reconstructive complexity rather than being directly compared for treatment superiority. Personalized free flap The results of this study demonstrate certain advantages over traditional treatment methods, such as the Masquelet technique. Chen et al. [ ] reported in a previous clinical study that the combination of 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation and the Masquelet technique for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis achieved a treatment success rate of 76.9% (10/13). They then preliminarily explored the efficacy of local pedicled flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation for treating tibial infected bone defects, with a treatment success rate of less than 60% (53.8%, 7/13 cases) [ ]. Notably, the incidence of flap-related complications in that study was 30.8%, which may have been due to poor blood supply and excessive tension at the flap margins. In contrast, we did not observe any cases of free flap transplantation failure or related complications. The

They then preliminarily explored the efficacy of local pedicled flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation for treating tibial infected bone defects, with a treatment success rate of less than 60% (53.8%, 7/13 cases) [ ]. Notably, the incidence of flap-related complications in that study was 30.8%, which may have been due to poor blood supply and excessive tension at the flap margins. In contrast, we did not observe any cases of free flap transplantation failure or related complications. The second-stage prosthesis implantation surgery was performed on average 4.8 ± 1.4 months after the first-stage free flap transplantation surgery. Innovatively, we used a personalized free flap (free anterolateral thigh flap) for repairing complex and large soft tissue defects, while also expanding the bone defect area from lower limb to limb-wide infected bone defects. By implementing precise infection control strategies (vancomycin-loaded bone cement release + pathogen-guided antibiotic therapy), we further enhanced the therapeutic efficacy, and the study preliminarily verified the feasibility of staged treatment (first-stage infection control combined with flap repair of soft tissue defects, second-stage mechanical reconstruction) for complex infected bone defects. Although the anterolateral thigh flap was the preferred option in the present series, alternative free flaps may be indicated depending on the characteristics of the defect and patient-related factors. The latissimus dorsi flap provides a large volume of well-vascularized tissue and is suitable for extensive soft tissue defects [ ]. The radial forearm flap offers thin and pliable coverage for smaller defects requiring contour precision [ ]. The gracilis flap may be considered for moderate-sized defects when a shorter operative time and limited donor-site morbidity are desired [ ]. In selected cases, a free fibular flap can simultaneously address segmental bone loss and soft tissue defects, although its use may be limited in the setting of infection or compromised recipient vessels [ ]. Therefore, free flap selection should be individualized based on defect size, location, infection status, and reconstructive goals. Diabetes and recurrent infections Regarding postoperative complications, the overall complication rate was 10% (8/80), with recurrent infection (7.5%) and prosthesis and screw mechanical fractures (2.5%) being the most common. Among them, two diabetic patients with extensive dorsal foot soft tissue defects accompanied by large metatarsal bone defects both experienced recurrent infections postoperatively, and one diabetic patient had a recurrent tibial infection. Univariate logistic regression analysis showed that a history of diabetes was significantly associated with a higher risk of any complications and recurrent infection ( p < 0.05), which drew our attention to diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Previous studies have shown that in diabetic patients, the significant changes in ischemia and neuropathy are primarily in the foot, which greatly increases the risk of foot bone infection [ , ]. In response, our experience suggests that preoperative strict control of HbA1c (≤ 7.5%) and serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L should be prioritized. After microporous titanium implantation, we extended the antibiotic regimen to 8 weeks (instead of the usual 2 weeks) and used dynamic follow-up with infection markers to monitor recurrent infections. For the 3 cases of recurrent infection in diabetic patients, the medical team conducted detailed discussions and analyses, discovering that patients had not received standardized foot care after discharge, which may have contributed to the infection recurrence. Additionally, all three patients had varying degrees of peripheral vascular disease, which posed a challenge to flap survival and the growth environment. Therefore, we recommend that before surgical treatment of diabetic osteomyelitis patients, classification according to guidelines (high risk, low risk, or moderate risk), such as the DFU prevention and management guidelines published by the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) [ ], should be conducted to facilitate targeted, stratified treatment. Diabetes is known to impair immune function, microcirculation, and wound healing, which may contribute to persistent or recurrent infection [ ]. In our clinical practice, diabetes was not considered a contraindication to microporous titanium implantation or free flap reconstruction; however, these patients were managed as a high-risk subgroup. Management strategies included strict preoperative glycemic control, optimization of nutritional and metabolic status, thorough and staged debridement when necessary, and close postoperative surveillance for early signs of infection recurrence [ , ]. Multidisciplinary collaboration with endocrinologists and infected disease specialists was routinely employed. These measures may help mitigate infection-related risks in diabetic patients, although careful patient selection and individualized treatment planning remain essential. Moreover, Metaoy et al. [ ] found that local use of antibiotic-loaded implants can increase the eradication rate of infection in diabetic foot osteomyelitis and may further reduce amputation and mortality rates. Another meta-analysis showed that diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients treated with local antibiotic delivery systems had significantly higher healing rates compared to the control group [ ].

These measures may help mitigate infection-related risks in diabetic patients, although careful patient selection and individualized treatment planning remain essential. Moreover, Metaoy et al. [ ] found that local use of antibiotic-loaded implants can increase the eradication rate of infection in diabetic foot osteomyelitis and may further reduce amputation and mortality rates. Another meta-analysis showed that diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients treated with local antibiotic delivery systems had significantly higher healing rates compared to the control group [ ]. In this regard, developing a local antibiotic delivery system on the surface of microporous titanium or modifying it for controlled drug release could be an effective strategy for treating diabetic foot infected bone defects. Nevertheless, the retrospective design of this study inevitably introduces the risk of selection bias and limits the ability to draw causal inferences. In contrast, a prospective study design would enable predefined inclusion criteria, standardized data collection, and uniform follow-up protocols, thereby improving data completeness and internal validity. Future prospective studies or registries are therefore warranted to further validate the clinical effectiveness and safety of 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses in the management of infected bone defects. Additionally, from a clinical applicability perspective, several practical factors merit consideration, including cost, operative duration, and prosthesis manufacturing time. Patient-specific 3D-printed titanium prostheses generally involve higher upfront costs and require a manufacturing period for design and printing [ , ]. However, these factors may be balanced by potential clinical advantages, such as reduced need for staged reconstruction, earlier weight-bearing, and avoidance of prolonged external fixation in selected cases. Operative duration is primarily influenced by the extent of bone and soft tissue defects and the need for combined free flap reconstruction, rather than by prosthesis implantation alone. Future studies incorporating standardized cost-effectiveness and workflow analyses are needed to further define the role of this technique in routine clinical practice. Limitations This study has several limitations: (1) The retrospective design may introduce recall bias, and the lack of a control group (such as comparisons with traditional Masquelet or Ilizarov technique) may lead to selection bias. Future studies should include prospective randomized controlled trials to verify long-term efficacy while expanding the sample size; (2) The cases in this study are still concentrated in the early to mid-term follow-up, lacking long-term follow-up data beyond 10 years, which makes it difficult to assess prosthesis wear and the risk of late loosening; (3) A limitation of this study is the absence of a validated upper-extremity functional outcome measure, such as the DASH or QuickDASH questionnaire. This was primarily due to the very small number of upper-extremity cases in the combined free flap group ( n = 3), which would have rendered meaningful statistical analysis underpowered and potentially misleading. Future prospective studies with larger, multi-center cohorts are needed to allow balanced anatomical representation and comprehensive limb-specific functional evaluation (4). Risk factor exploration was based on univariate logistic regression only. Given the small number of events, multivariable modeling was not performed to avoid overfitting. Future studies with larger event numbers should apply multivariable regression to better control for confounding. Despite these limitations, this study represents the largest cohort of patients to date who underwent 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation or combined free flap repair and reconstruction for infected bone defects of the limbs, with or without soft tissue defects. The average follow-up of 40.8 months provides preliminary evidence for the feasibility and universality of personalized customization and staged treatment. In conclusion, 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses (either alone or combined with free flaps) provide a reliable staged solution for limb infected bone defects. Throughout the follow-up period (≥ 3 months), both the single microporous titanium group and the free flap combined group maintained continuous improvements in pain relief and lower limb function. However, larger-sample and longer-term randomized controlled trials are still required in the future to validate the feasibility and safety of this surgical approach. documents.title: IWGDF guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are among the most serious chronic complications of diabetes, with a lifetime incidence of up to 34% ( ) and an increasingly younger affected population. DFUs arise from the interplay of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), and impaired immune function, typically presenting as skin breakdown, infection, or tissue necrosis that may extend to bone or joints. These lesions markedly increase the risk of amputation—with reported rates up to 33%—and lead to disability in approximately 20% of patients ( , ), representing a major public health challenge. Once a DFU becomes infected, the resulting diabetic foot infection (DFI) usually begins with microbial colonization following disruption of the skin barrier and progresses under conditions of hyperglycemia, microvascular dysfunction, and impaired neutrophil activity ( ). Notably, the clinical manifestations of DFI may be masked by neuropathy, PAD, or immunosuppression; some patients develop deep tissue involvement or osteomyelitis without typical signs of inflammation ( , ). Thus, infection assessment should not rely solely on culture results but must integrate wound characteristics, systemic symptoms, and imaging evidence ( ). The severity of DFI is closely related to its anatomical spread. The foot’s fascial compartments facilitate proximal extension of infection along tendons and fascial planes. When inflammatory pressure increases within these closed spaces, ischemic necrosis may ensue, accelerating disease progression ( , ). Patients with chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled diabetes, or recurrent ulcers are at even higher risk for necrotizing or systemic infections ( ). Although many infections begin superficially, without timely intervention, they may rapidly invade deeper soft tissues, joints, or bone, posing a serious threat to limb and life ( ). Current international guidelines recommend staging DFIs based on infection extent, depth, and systemic involvement, and tailoring treatment accordingly—including antimicrobial therapy, debridement, revascularization, and multidisciplinary management ( ). However, large-scale, stratified clinical evidence on stage-based treatment of infected DFUs remains limited in China. To address this gap, we retrospectively analyzed 300 patients with DFU-associated infections using the IWGDF/IDSA classification system ( , ) to stratify infection severity, guide individualized treatment, and evaluate clinical outcomes. This study aims to provide evidence for standardized, stepwise management of DFIs, optimize treatment pathways, reduce amputation rates, and improve patient prognosis. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design This was a single-center, retrospective observational cohort study. The study aimed to systematically evaluate the real-world application, microbiological characteristics, treatment response, and long-term clinical outcomes of a stage-based treatment strategy guided by the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot/Infectious Diseases Society of America (IWGDF/IDSA) clinical classification system in patients with diabetic foot infection (DFI). The study protocol was designed and conducted in strict accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and received formal approval from the hospital’s Institutional Review Board prior to initiation (Approval No. 2019–701). As this study involved secondary analysis of existing, anonymized clinical data without new interventions, and all data collection and processing adhered to strict confidentiality agreements, the ethics committee granted a waiver for obtaining individual patient informed consent. However, all patients admitted to the hospital had signed a general consent form permitting the use of their de-identified medical data for retrospective medical research. 2.2 Study subjects and screening process 2.2.1 Study population and source The study population consisted of consecutive patients who presented to the hospital’s Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Vascular Surgery, and Wound Care Center between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024 for diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) complicated by infection. Potential subjects were initially identified through the hospital’s electronic medical record system using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes for diabetic foot and related complications, supplemented by cross-referencing departmental inpatient and outpatient registries to ensure comprehensive inclusion. 2.2.2 Sample size estimation To ensure adequate statistical power, a formal sample size calculation was performed during the study design phase. Based on preliminary literature review and pilot data from our center, we assumed a 6-month ulcer non-healing rate of approximately 40% in patients with moderate infection (Grade 3). To detect a clinically meaningful absolute difference of at least 15% in healing rates between different infection grades (e.g., Grade 2 vs. Grade 4) with a two-sided significance level ( α ) of 0.05 and a power (1-β) of 80%, the formula for comparing two proportions was used. The calculation indicated a requirement of at least 70–90 patients per major comparison group. Considering the planned division into four subgroups and subsequent multivariate analyses, to avoid underpowered analyses, the total sample size target was set at 300 patients. This number was deemed sufficient not only for the primary analyses but also for the planned subgroup analyses and predictive model development. 2.2.3 Inclusion and exclusion criteria Explicit, operational inclusion and exclusion criteria were established. All initially screened medical records were independently reviewed by two researchers. Inclusion Criteria: Age ≥18 years. A confirmed diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus, with a documented disease duration of more than 6 months. Presence of an active, full-thickness skin ulcer distal to the ankle, persisting for at least 2 weeks. Clinical diagnosis of diabetic foot infection, defined as the target ulcer exhibiting at least two of the following local signs or symptoms of inflammation (erythema extending beyond the ulcer margin, swelling, tenderness or spontaneous pain, purulent discharge, or markedly increased local warmth) in the absence of alternative non-infectious explanations (e.g., acute exacerbation of a purely neuropathic ulcer, Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy, and tophus ulceration). Availability of complete electronic medical records from admission through follow-up, with no missing key data (demographics, laboratory tests, imaging reports, treatment regimens, and post-discharge follow-up records), and a minimum effective post-operative or post-discharge follow-up period of 4 weeks. Exclusion Criteria were designed to exclude conditions that might confound infection assessment, treatment response, or outcome determination: Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, gestational diabetes, or other specific types of diabetes. Foot lesions definitively attributable to non-infectious etiologies, such as uninfected pure neuropathic ulcers, acute Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy, skin breakdown due to acute gout, and psoriatic lesions. Primary or metastatic malignancy at the ulcer site, or radiation-induced ulcers. Pregnancy or lactation. Severe psychiatric illness, dementia, or other cognitive impairment precluding reliable clinical assessment or history provision. Missing key information in the medical records required to determine the IWGDF/IDSA infection grade, unclear initial antimicrobial regimen, or undetermined primary outcome status (healing/amputation). 2.2.4 Screening flowchart and final cohort The screening process strictly adhered to the pre-specified criteria and was clearly illustrated using a flowchart ( ). Of the 386 initially identified potentially eligible patients, 300 were ultimately included in the final analysis cohort after sequential screening. Major reasons for exclusion and corresponding numbers were as follows: 38 patients did not meet the clinical diagnostic criteria for DFI (e.g., simple ulcer without clear signs of infection); 25 patients had critical missing baseline data (e.g., HbA1c and vascular examination results) or follow-up information; 15 patients had incomplete or contradictory clinical/imaging evidence required for infection severity grading; and 8 patients met other exclusion criteria (e.g., concomitant lower limb tumor [ n = 3], pregnancy [ n = 2], and severe cognitive impairment [ n = 3]). The final cohort of 300 patients constituted the study population and was allocated into four study subgroups based on their admission infection severity. 2.3 Data collection and variable definitions 2.3.1 Data sources and collection process All data were retrospectively extracted from the hospital’s comprehensive electronic information systems, including the electronic medical record system, laboratory information system, picture archiving and communication system, and surgical anesthesia system. To ensure accuracy and consistency, a standardized data collection form was designed. Data extraction was performed independently by two trained research coordinators not involved in the clinical management of the patients. Discrepancies or contradictions in the records were resolved by consulting original documentation, consulting the attending physician, or arbitration by a third senior researcher. 2.3.2 Baseline characteristics and clinical variables Collected baseline data included: (1) Demographics : age, sex. (2) Diabetes-related metrics : duration of diabetes, most recent glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) value, current glucose-lowering regimen. (3) Comorbidities : Presence of hypertension, chronic kidney disease (defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 according to KDIGO guidelines), peripheral arterial disease (diagnosed based on history, physical examination, and/or ABI/TBI ≤ 0.9), and peripheral neuropathy (based on symptoms, signs, and/or neurophysiological testing) were confirmed using diagnostic codes and medication records. (4) Ulcer characteristics : location, size, duration, Wagner grade (if applicable). (5) Infection-related indicators : Body temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin levels at admission. 2.3.3 Microbiological evaluation All microbiological specimens were obtained via sharp surgical debridement from deep tissue or bone, with strict avoidance of superficial swabs. Whenever clinically feasible, specimens were collected prior to the initiation of antimicrobial therapy. For patients who had already received antibiotics prior to admission or in whom discontinuation of therapy was not clinically safe (particularly those with severe infections presenting with systemic inflammatory response syndrome), specimens were obtained at the time of the first surgical debridement after admission, and the timing of specimen collection relative to antibiotic administration (pre-treatment, during treatment, or post-treatment) was recorded for subsequent sensitivity analysis. Specimens were promptly delivered to the clinical microbiology laboratory for standard aerobic and anaerobic culture, species identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (using disk diffusion or broth microdilution methods). All isolated pathogens and their susceptibility profiles were recorded. Polymicrobial infection was defined as the isolation of two or more pathogenic microorganisms from the same specimen. Polymicrobial infection was defined as the isolation of two or more distinct pathogenic microorganisms from the same deep tissue specimen obtained under aseptic conditions during surgical debridement. To ensure that isolates represented true pathogens rather than colonizers or contaminants, the following criteria were applied: (1) Specimen quality requirements: All specimens were obtained via sharp surgical debridement from deep viable tissue (not superficial swabs), after thorough wound cleansing and removal of all exudate and necrotic tissue. Specimens were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy whenever clinically feasible, or the timing of antibiotic exposure was recorded. (2) Quantitative thresholds: Isolates were considered clinically significant if they demonstrated growth above laboratory-defined thresholds (typically ≥10 4 CFU/g for tissue specimens) and were morphologically consistent on culture media. (3) Clinical correlation: Isolates were classified as contaminants if they represented typical skin commensals (e.g., coagulase-negative staphylococci, Corynebacterium species, Cutibacterium acnes , and Micrococcus species) in the absence of clinical signs of invasive infection or if they were present only in small numbers alongside dominant pathogens. Conversely, organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus , Streptococcus species, Enterococcus species, Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and obligate anaerobes were consistently regarded as potential pathogens when isolated from appropriate specimens. (4) Repeat isolation: When available, consistent isolation of the same organism from multiple specimens or correlation with Gram stain findings (e.g., presence of neutrophils with intracellular bacteria) supported its designation as a true pathogen. All culture results were interpreted in conjunction with the patient’s clinical presentation, inflammatory markers, and response to therapy. Cases with ambiguous microbiological findings were reviewed by a multidisciplinary team including infectious disease specialists and clinical microbiologists to reach consensus on pathogen significance. All Staphylococcus aureus isolates were tested for methicillin resistance using both phenotypic and genotypic methods. Phenotypic detection was performed by the cefoxitin disk diffusion method (30 μg) on Mueller–Hinton agar, with results interpreted according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines (zone diameter ≤21 mm indicating MRSA). For genotypic confirmation, multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was employed to detect the presence of the mecA gene, which encodes the altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) responsible for methicillin resistance. DNA extraction was performed using a boiling lysis method, and PCR amplification targeted the mecA gene (primers: forward 5′-AAAACTAGGTGTTGGTGAAGATATACC-3′, reverse 5′-GAAAGGATCTGTACTGGGTTAATCAG-3′; product size 147 bp). Isolates were classified as MRSA if they demonstrated resistance by cefoxitin disk diffusion and/or tested positive for the mecA gene. Discrepancies between phenotypic and genotypic results were resolved by repeat testing and, if necessary, PBP2a latex agglutination assay. Deep tissue and bone specimens were obtained during sharp surgical debridement, placed immediately into sterile containers with sterile saline, and transported to the microbiology laboratory within 2 h for processing. Routine anaerobic culture protocols and dedicated anaerobic transport systems (e.g., Robertson’s cooked meat medium) were not employed. While this method supports recovery of aerobic and facultative anaerobic organisms, it is suboptimal for strict anaerobes and likely contributed to their underdetection in our cohort, particularly in deep infections and osteomyelitis, where anaerobes are commonly implicated. All aerobic and facultative anaerobic isolates were identified using standard microbiological techniques. Gram-positive cocci were identified by colony morphology, Gram stain, catalase test, coagulase test (for Staphylococcus aureus ), and optochin susceptibility or bile solubility (for Streptococcus pneumoniae ). Gram-negative bacilli were identified using conventional biochemical panels (e.g., oxidase test, indole test, urease test, citrate utilization, and triple sugar iron agar reactions) and, for a subset of isolates, the VITEK 2 automated system (bioMérieux, France) or API identification strips (bioMérieux). Species-level identification was performed for all clinically significant isolates. For anaerobic organisms, as detailed above, dedicated anaerobic cultures were not routinely performed; therefore, no anaerobic isolates were available for identification. (2) Revascularization : Whether the patient underwent lower extremity arterial intervention (e.g., angioplasty and stenting) or bypass surgery, and the timing. (3) Antimicrobial therapy : Drug class, dosage, and route of administration for initial empirical therapy; subsequent adjustments based on susceptibility results; total duration of treatment. (4) Wound adjunctive therapies : Type of dressing used (e.g., hydrocolloid, alginate, and silver-containing), application of negative pressure wound therapy, and its duration. (5) Systemic supportive care : Glycemic control protocol and achieved target ranges. 2.4 Infection severity grading (core exposure variable) Infection severity served as the core stratification variable, assessed using the internationally recognized IWGDF/IDSA clinical classification system. The assessment was conducted within 24 h of admission by a multidisciplinary team comprising at least an endocrinologist, an infectious disease specialist, and a vascular surgeon. All team members received uniform training on the grading system. Grading was based on a complete history, physical examination, and preliminary laboratory and imaging findings, using the following specific criteria: Grade 2 (Mild) : Infection confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissue around the ulcer, with erythema extending <2 cm from the ulcer margin, and no clinical or imaging evidence of involvement of deep structures (e.g., fascia, muscle, tendon, joint, and bone). The patient has no systemic signs or symptoms of infection. Grade 3 (Moderate) : Infection is more extensive, manifested by erythema ≥2 cm from the ulcer margin, and/or infection involves the aforementioned deep tissues, but the patient does not exhibit systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Grade 3(O) (Moderate with Osteomyelitis) : The criteria for Grade 3 infection were met, with a definitive diagnosis of osteomyelitis confirmed by imaging (magnetic resonance imaging or radionuclide bone scan) and/or a positive probe-to-bone test, but the patient still lacks SIRS. Osteomyelitis was diagnosed according to IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guidelines based on a combination of clinical, imaging, and intraoperative findings. Diagnosis required at least two of the following: (1) a positive probe-to-bone test (palpation of hard, gritty bone at the ulcer base using a sterile metal probe); (2) definitive imaging evidence, preferably on MRI (bone marrow edema on T2-weighted images with corresponding low T1 signal, cortical disruption, or intraosseous abscess) or, when MRI was contraindicated, plain radiography or radionuclide bone scanning showing cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, or sequestrum; (3) intraoperative findings of grossly infected or necrotic bone, or bone failing to bleed when cut (“paprika sign”); or (4) histopathological confirmation (inflammatory infiltrate within bone marrow spaces or osteonecrosis) when bone specimens were obtained. All patients classified as Grade 3(O) met these criteria in the setting of moderate soft tissue infection without systemic inflammatory response syndrome. Grade 4 (Severe) : Foot infection accompanied by systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), defined by the presence of two or more of the following: ① Temperature >38 °C or <36 °C; ②

or radionuclide bone scanning showing cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, or sequestrum; (3) intraoperative findings of grossly infected or necrotic bone, or bone failing to bleed when cut (“paprika sign”); or (4) histopathological confirmation (inflammatory infiltrate within bone marrow spaces or osteonecrosis) when bone specimens were obtained. All patients classified as Grade 3(O) met these criteria in the setting of moderate soft tissue infection without systemic inflammatory response syndrome. Grade 4 (Severe) : Foot infection accompanied by systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), defined by the presence of two or more of the following: ① Temperature >38 °C or <36 °C; ② Heart rate >90 beats per minute; ③ Respiratory rate >20 breaths per minute or arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO₂) < 32 mmHg; ④ White blood cell count >12,000/μL or <4,000/μL, or >10% immature neutrophils (band forms). All cases of osteomyelitis with SIRS were classified as Grade 4. This grading result served as the basis for all subsequent subgroup analyses and model construction. We classified patients with moderate infection and confirmed osteomyelitis as a distinct subgroup (Grade 3[O]) for the following reasons: (1) to enable precise analysis of the prognostic impact of osteomyelitis independent of soft tissue infection extent, and (2) to evaluate whether this subgroup warrants distinct management strategies, as suggested by previous studies demonstrating poorer outcomes in patients with bone involvement. For severe infections with osteomyelitis, these patients were classified as Grade 4 (severe) per standard criteria, as the presence of SIRS supersedes the local finding of osteomyelitis in determining treatment urgency. 2.5 Outcome measures 2.5.1 Primary outcomes Ulcer Healing : Defined as complete re-epithelialization covering the entire ulcer bed without any exudate, maintained for at least 4 weeks after cessation of all specialized wound therapies. The healing date was defined as the date when complete epithelialization was first observed and was independently verified by two physicians blinded to patient grouping. Amputation : Categorized as minor amputation (amputation level distal to the ankle joint, including toe, partial foot, or transmetatarsal amputation) or major amputation (amputation level at or proximal to the ankle joint, including below-knee and above-knee amputation). The date and level of the first amputation procedure were recorded. Infection Control : Served as an early indicator of treatment response, defined as the normalization of body temperature (<37.3 °C) and a reduction of at least 50% from the peak value in systemic inflammatory markers (white blood cell count or C-reactive protein) within 72 h of initiating antimicrobial therapy. 2.5.2 Secondary outcomes Length of Hospital Stay : Number of days from the date of admission to the date of discharge. 30-Day Reinfection Rate : Occurrence of new signs of infection at the original ulcer site or adjacent area within 30 days after discharge, necessitating re-initiation of systemic antimicrobial therapy or surgical intervention. Treatment-Related Adverse Events : Clinically adverse events directly attributable to antimicrobial agents used during the study period were recorded, such as Clostridioides difficile -associated diarrhea, drug-induced liver injury (elevated liver enzymes >3 times the upper limit of normal), rash, or allergic reactions. 2.6 Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics software (Version 26.0) and the R statistical computing environment (version 4.3.1). All hypothesis tests were two-sided, and a p -value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Continuous variables conforming to a normal distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and compared between groups using one-way analysis of variance, with post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., LSD test) if overall significance was found. For continuous variables not conforming to a normal distribution or ordinal categorical variables, data are presented as median and interquartile range, and compared using the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis H test. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages, and compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test (when expected frequencies were <5). To analyze the long-term dynamic impact of infection grade on ulcer healing and limb preservation, we employed both standard survival methods and competing risk models. Time-zero definition : The date of hospital admission and initiation of standardized treatment was defined as time zero. Ulcer healing analysis: The endpoint event was achieving complete healing. Patients who remained unhealed at the study cutoff date or were lost to follow-up were censored. Death prior to healing was treated as a competing event in sensitivity analyses. Amputation analysis: For amputation outcomes, we recognized that death precludes the possibility of amputation and, therefore, represents a competing risk event, not simply a censoring event. Amputation analysis: For amputation outcomes, we recognized that death precludes the possibility of amputation and, therefore, represents a competing risk event, not simply a censoring event. Accordingly, we employed two complementary approaches. (1) Kaplan–Meier analysis (standard approach and death censored): We performed standard Kaplan–Meier survival analysis with amputation at any level as the endpoint. In this analysis, patients who died, were lost to follow-up, or remained amputation-free at study end were censored. Cumulative amputation-free survival curves were plotted for each infection grade, and the log-rank test was used to compare distributions between groups. (2) Competing risk analysis (Fine-Gray model, death as competing event): To account for death as a competing event, we performed Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models to estimate the cumulative incidence function (CIF) for amputation across infection grades. In these models, death without prior amputation was treated as a competing event, while loss to follow-up was treated as censoring. The Fine-Gray model provides unbiased estimates of the actual probability of amputation over time, accounting for the fact that patients who die are no longer at risk. Cumulative event (healing) curves and cumulative survival (amputation-free survival) curves were plotted for each infection grade (2, 3, 3(O), 4), accompanied by 95% confidence intervals. The log-rank test was used to compare survival distributions between different grade groups. Univariate and multivariate Cox models were constructed to calculate hazard ratios and their 95% confidence intervals for different infection grades relative to the reference group (Grade 2), quantifying the magnitude of risk. The proportional hazards assumption of the models was verified by testing the correlation of Schoenfeld residuals with time. The outcome variable for nomogram development was the binary variable “non-healing within 6 months,” defined as failure to achieve complete epithelialization of the index ulcer within 24 weeks (168 days) from time zero. This definition encompassed two clinical scenarios: (1) patients whose ulcers remained unhealed at the 24-week follow-up assessment; and (2) patients who underwent amputation (minor or major) prior to achieving complete healing, as amputation precludes the possibility of ulcer healing. For patients who died within the 24-week follow-up period without prior amputation and without achieving healing, they were classified as non-healed in the primary analysis (worst-case scenario), with sensitivity analyses treating death as a competing event as described above. Patients who were lost to follow-up before 24 weeks without documented healing or amputation were excluded from the nomogram development cohort. Initial candidate predictors included all baseline clinical and laboratory variables associated with non-healing in univariate analyses ( p < 0.10). A multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression framework was used. Final independent predictors were selected via forward stepwise regression (based on the likelihood ratio test, with inclusion criteria p < 0.05 and exclusion criteria p > 0.10) to ensure a parsimonious and clinically usable model. Using the rms package in R, the regression coefficients of each predictor in the final Cox model were proportionally converted into a 0–100 point scoring system. The total score was then mapped to the predicted 6-month probability of non-healing, resulting in a visual nomogram. The concordance index and its 95% confidence interval were calculated for the model in the training set. A C-index closer to 1 indicates a better ability to discriminate between patients with different prognoses. A calibration curve was plotted. Patients were grouped into deciles based on their predicted risk. The mean predicted probability and the actual observed Kaplan–Meier estimated probability for each decile were calculated, and their agreement assessed. The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test was also performed. Bootstrap resampling (1,000 repetitions) was used for internal validation of the model. The bootstrap-corrected C-index was calculated to reduce overfitting and provide a more objective estimate of the model’s expected performance on new data.
