documents.title: IWGDF Guideline on Wound Healing Interventions in Diabetic Foot

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Diabetic foot is a serious complication of diabetes with high morbidity and mortality rates [ ], affecting 6.3% of the diabetic population, including 5.5% in Asia and Iran [ ]. DFU is one of the most complex and heterogeneous complications of diabetes; however, its management is hindered by the lack of a universally accepted and clinically practical classification system [ ]. Although many efforts have been made in recent years to develop international guidelines to provide standard care, data on outcomes and predictors in patients with DFU are limited [ ]. Several classification systems have been devised to enable effective comparison of clinical outcomes; however, almost all of these systems have limitations and there is no universally agreed upon standard [ ]. The International Working Group on Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) has systematically reviewed 28 wound classification tools across 149 articles. Most studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias, often reporting only unadjusted associations. Based on this review, the IWGDF identified six classification systems with relatively better performance in associational analyses of wound outcomes, while emphasising each system has its own limitations [ , ]. These classification systems include Maggit‐Wagner, SINBAD (ulcer Site, Ischemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial infection, Area and Depth), University of Texas Wound Classification System (UTWCS), Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) classification system, WIFI (Wound, Ischemia, Foot Infection) and DiaFORA (diabetic foot risk assessment tool) [ ]. IWGDF recommends the use of the SINBAD system for communication between healthcare staff to manage ulcers and suggests the WIFI system if resources permit. However, they have stated that the conditions in which the classification system is supposed to be applied are not always clear, and current recommendations regarding the use of these systems are different based on societies, countries and the availability of procedures and specialised staff, so it is strongly recommended to conduct more validation studies [ , ]. Current validation studies have primarily relied on generalised linear models, such as logistic regression and Cox proportional hazard models, to predict wound healing outcomes, which may not effectively capture the complex nature of DFUs [ , , ]. In contrast, machine learning algorithms, a branch of artificial intelligence, have gained recognition for their diagnostic and prognostic capabilities, often outperforming traditional linear models in various applications [ ]. Given the complexity and heterogeneity of wound characteristics and patient profiles, the integration of machine learning techniques is increasingly seen as a high priority in this field [ , ]. Despite this, our knowledge indicates that previous validation studies of wound classification systems have not adequately employed advanced machine learning methods to evaluate the prognostic outcomes associated with each classification system. This gap underscores the need for innovative approaches that leverage machine learning to enhance the predictive power and clinical utility of existing DFU classification systems. In this study, we initially validated the six IWGDF‐approved classification systems and assessed their predictive power for poor wound prognosis using machine learning algorithms in a prospective cohort study. Finally, to improve the performance of the existing classification systems or simplify their application, we proposed modifications to the well‐performing systems. 2 Material and Methods 2.1 Study Design and Participants This prospective cohort study was conducted at the outpatient wound clinic of Tehran University of Medical Sciences. The cohort has been described previously in a study evaluating the prediction of amputation using diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) classification systems [ ]. Briefly, patients with newly diagnosed DFUs were consecutively enrolled after providing written informed consent and followed for 6 months. Baseline demographic characteristics, diabetes‐related factors, comorbidities, laboratory markers, medication use and wound characteristics relevant to outpatient care were collected by trained physicians and nurses using a standardised checklist, as previously reported [ ]. In the present study, six IWGDF‐endorsed wound classification systems (PEDIS, SINBAD, Wagner, UTWCS, WIFI and DiaFORA) were evaluated for their ability to predict non‐healing, representing a distinct clinical application from the prior amputation‐focused analysis. 2.2 Outcome Definition The binary outcome was defined as follows: Non‐healed (Class 1): failure to achieve complete wound healing within 6 months of baseline assessment, including patients who underwent minor or major amputation during follow‐up. Healed (Class 0): complete wound healing, defined as full epithelialization of the skin 2.3 Statistical Analysis Before doing any modifications on wound classification systems and compare their performance to predict DFU poor prognosis with original tools, in the first part, we determined the prediction power of the classification system. For this purpose, first associations between each classification system and non‐healing were assessed using univariate logistic regression. Multivariable prediction models were then developed using 10 machine learning algorithms. Each classification system was entered as the primary predictor and adjusted for relevant clinical variables. 2.3 Statistical Analysis Before doing any modifications on wound classification systems and compare their performance to predict DFU poor prognosis with original tools, in the first part, we determined the prediction power of the classification system. For this purpose, first associations between each classification system and non‐healing were assessed using univariate logistic regression. Multivariable prediction models were then developed using 10 machine learning algorithms. Each classification system was entered as the primary predictor and adjusted for relevant clinical variables. The machine learning algorithms used in this study included random forest, decision trees, support vector machines (SVM), including radial basis function (RBF) and linear SVM, XGBoost, K‐nearest neighbours (KNN), Gaussian process, Naïve Bayes, logistic regression and deep neural networks. The data was divided into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%). Hyperparameter tuning was performed for deep neural networks, XGBoost, random forest and SVM algorithms, utilising fivefold cross‐validation. The architecture of the neural networks is detailed in the appendix file. The reported performance was based on test data. To reduce overfitting, feature selection was performed using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) and random forest methods. To prevent data leakage, the dataset was first split into training and test sets and then feature selection was applied separately on the train and test sets. Algorithms included random forest, decision tree, XGBoost, SVM (linear and RBF), K‐nearest neighbours, Gaussian process, Naïve Bayes, logistic regression and deep neural networks. For each classification system, three feature sets were evaluated: Reduced model (random forest selection), reduced model (LASSO) and Full model (all predictors). The best‐performing method among the three feature sets was then used for the final comparison of wound classification systems. Hyperparameter tuning using fivefold cross‐validation was performed for algorithms with substantial model complexity and tuning sensitivity, including deep neural networks, XGBoost, random forest and support vector machines with linear and radial basis function kernels. For other algorithms—logistic regression, Naïve Bayes, Gaussian process classifiers and decision trees—default or standard parameter settings were used, as these algorithms have limited tunable parameters and extensive tuning may lead to overfitting in a dataset of this size. Since the outcome distribution was moderately imbalanced (64.6% healed and 35.4% non‐healed ulcers), several strategies were evaluated to address class imbalance during model development. We first explored data‐level approaches, including oversampling, under sampling and the Synthetic Minority Over‐sampling Technique (SMOTE). However, these methods did not improve model generalisation and, in some cases, reduced performance on the independent test set. Consequently, we adopted algorithm‐level strategies to handle class imbalance. For deep neural network models, binary cross‐entropy with logits loss (BCEWithLogitsLoss) with class weighting was used to penalise misclassification of the minority (non‐healed) class. For other machine learning algorithms, class imbalance was addressed using class‐weighted loss functions or balanced class weights, where supported by the algorithm. To provide a complete evaluation of model performance under imbalance, we report per‐class metrics for the non‐healed class (positive class) including precision, recall (sensitivity) and F1‐score, in addition to specificity and AUC. These metrics are presented in Tables , , and refer to Class 1 = non‐healed ulcers. This approach ensures that model performance is assessed fairly for the clinically important non‐healed outcome, rather than relying solely on accuracy, which can be misleading in imbalanced datasets. Because some patients contributed more than one ulcer, we accounted for within‐patient clustering during model development. To avoid data leakage and violation of independence assumptions, training and test sets were created at the patient level rather than the ulcer level. Specifically, a group‐based data splitting strategy was applied, in which all ulcers from the same patient were assigned exclusively to either the training set or the test set. This approach ensured that no patient contributed ulcers to both datasets and prevented inflation of predictive performance estimates. In the second part of the study, to improve the performance of the existing classification systems to predict unhealing outcomes in outpatient services, we proposed modifications to the WIFI, SINBAD and DiaFORA as follows: First Proposed WIFI Model : The original WIFI model was modified by replacing the ischemia and wound components with revised definitions. The ischemia component was refined as peripheral pulses and ABI instead of only ABI index, and the wound depth was redefined using three categories, as score 1 (superficial wound), score 2 (muscle involvement), score 3 (deep wound to tendon, bone or joint). Second Proposed WIFI Model : This model only incorporated the revised wound depth categories (as above) into the wound component. 2.4 Proposed Modification to the <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">SINBAD</styled-content> Classification Tool The original SINBAD model was enhanced by including detailed wound location (1: Forefoot—toes, 2: Forefoot—distal, 3: Metatarsal, 4: Hindfoot), replacing the original ischemia component with the Ankle‐Brachial Index (ABI) and the infection component with the IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) classification. 2.5 Proposed Modifications to

Second Proposed WIFI Model : This model only incorporated the revised wound depth categories (as above) into the wound component. 2.4 Proposed Modification to the <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">SINBAD</styled-content> Classification Tool The original SINBAD model was enhanced by including detailed wound location (1: Forefoot—toes, 2: Forefoot—distal, 3: Metatarsal, 4: Hindfoot), replacing the original ischemia component with the Ankle‐Brachial Index (ABI) and the infection component with the IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) classification. 2.5 Proposed Modifications to the <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">DiaFORA</styled-content> Classification Tool First Proposed DiaFORA Model : The original model was revised by incorporating peripheral vascular disease defined via ABI and infection assessed using the IDSA classification. Second Proposed DiaFORA Model : This version added wound dimensions categorised as 1: < 1 cm 2 , 2: Between 1 and 3 cm 2 , 3: > 3 cm 2 . Third Proposed DiaFORA Model : This comprehensive model combined all enhancements: addition of peripheral vascular disease (via ABI), infection (via IDSA) and wound location (1‐forefoot: fingers 2‐forefoot: distal 3‐ metatarsal 4‐hindfoot). Performance of models evaluated using accuracy, AUC, precision (positive predictive value), recall (sensitivity), F1‐score and specificity as follows: Recall or sensitivity = True positive True positive + False Negative Specificity = True Negative False Positive + True Negative Precision = True positive True positive + False Positive Accuracy = True positive + True Negative True positive + True Negative + False Positive + False Negative F 1 – Score = 2 * True positive 2 * True positive + False Positive + False Negative 3 Results This study included 616 DFU for 400 participants, with a mean age of 60.8 (SD = 9.5), 61.3 (SD = 9.3) and 63.5 (SD = 9.9) years in the three groups of healed, unhealed and amputated patients, respectively. The majority of participants were men (66.9%), and within 6 months, the percentages of healing, non‐healing and amputation were 64.6%, 24.5% and 10.9%, respectively. In women, these rates were 82.4%, 12.2% and 5.4%, respectively. The characteristics of studied variables are summarised in Table . In the first step of validating each classification system, we evaluated the relationship between each classification system and outcome using univariate logistic regression. The results indicated, in all classification systems, the chance of unhealed wound increased significantly with increasing severity of wounds in terms of their respective stages. According to univariate logistic regression results, increasing wound severity in all classification systems was significantly associated with higher odds of non‐healing. In the Wagner classification, non‐healing risk increased with deeper tissue penetration and the presence of both infection and gangrene in stages 3 and 4. In the University of Texas (UT) classification, grade 3 wounds penetrating tendon, joint, or bone increased the odds of non‐healing within 6 months (OR = 4.3, 95% CI: 2.8–6.7). Wounds with simultaneous infection and ischemia in the UT system also had a higher risk of non‐healing (OR = 4.4, 95% CI: 2.4–7.8). For the SINBAD system, all components except neuropathy were significantly associated with non‐healing. The aggregate SINBAD score also correlated with increased risk: a score of 5 out of 6 corresponded to OR = 7.4 (95% CI: 3.0–18.3), and a score of 6 corresponded to OR = 10.0 (95% CI: 3.9–25.4). In the PEDIS classification, higher non‐healing risk was observed for more severe stages, including larger wound extent ( p = 0.012), deeper wounds ( p < 0.001), critical limb ischemia ( p < 0.001), deep tissue infection including osteomyelitis ( p < 0.001) and systemic infection ( p = 0.020) (Table ). The variables of neuropathy ( p = 0.289), mild infection ( p = 0.106), previous ulcer or amputation ( p = 0.200) and PAD ( p = 0.113) did not show significant relationships with healing status (Table ). The results of our analysis indicated that the univariate models demonstrated limited performance across the various wound classification systems (Table ). In the next step of the performance assessment of the classification systems, we used multivariate models using machine learning algorithms. We compared LASSO and random forest feature selection models with the full model for each classification system (as shown in Tables ). Details of the selected features for each feature selection method applied to the classification systems are provided in Table . In the next step, we identified the best algorithms for each classification system. These selected algorithms formed the basis for our comparative analysis of the classification systems. Tables present the performance of the six wound classification systems in predicting non‐healing outcomes over 6 months. For each classification system, 10 algorithms were evaluated in both full and reduced models. The best‐performing algorithm for each system was identified by comparing models across

In the next step, we identified the best algorithms for each classification system. These selected algorithms formed the basis for our comparative analysis of the classification systems. Tables present the performance of the six wound classification systems in predicting non‐healing outcomes over 6 months. For each classification system, 10 algorithms were evaluated in both full and reduced models. The best‐performing algorithm for each system was identified by comparing models across multiple indicators, including accuracy, sensitivity (recall), specificity, precision, F1 score and AUC. Greater weight was given to sensitivity and F1 score, as these metrics best reflect the ability to correctly identify non‐healing cases while balancing false positives and false negatives. For example, in Table , the logistic regression model with Random Forest–based feature selection outperformed both the LASSO‐based and full models. It achieved a higher F1 score (67.7 vs. 66.7), accuracy (63.6% vs. 59.5%) and specificity (80.2% vs. 75.2%) compared with the LASSO model and also surpassed the full model in accuracy (77.7% vs. 76.0%), sensitivity (72.4% vs. 60.9%) and specificity (80.2% vs. 77.7%) while using fewer variables. Based on these criteria, the Random Forest–reduced logistic regression model was selected as the optimal algorithm for evaluating the Wagner classification system. This same selection process was applied to the other classification systems, yielding one optimal algorithm for each. Table summarises these models and allows direct comparison across the six systems. As shown, the SINBAD and UTWCS systems demonstrated the strongest performance overall, with higher sensitivity (74.1 for SINBAD and 75.9 for UTWCS) and F1 scores (71.1 and 71.5, respectively) than the other systems, indicating a superior ability to predict non‐healing cases. Upon comparison of the wound classification systems, we proposed modifications to the criteria for each system to improve predictive performance or simplify implementation. The main modifications focused on the WIFI, SINBAD and DiaFORA systems (Table ). For example, in the WIFI system, the wound component was replaced with a depth grading system (score 1: superficial, score 2: muscle involvement, score 3: deep wound to tendon, bone, or joint). This change provided a more granular representation of wound severity, which allowed the models to better distinguish between patients with poor versus favorable prognoses according to reporting performance metrics (recall and F1‐score of 77.6% and 72.6% for new model compared to 70.7% and 68.9% of original WIFI model). For the SINBAD system, switching from a binary scoring approach to more detailed component scores did not meaningfully improve predictions, suggesting that additional granularity alone was insufficient without changing key risk predictors. Conversely, modifications to the DiaFORA system—particularly in model 2—incorporated more specific measures of ulcer size (PEDIS2) and peripheral arterial disease (ABI, IDSA), which enhanced the model's ability to identify individuals at high risk for poor outcomes. Overall, the multivariate models demonstrated that the WIFI model 2 modifications, which replaced the original wound component with depth grading, had the greatest impact on prediction. By providing a finer‐scale measurement of wound severity, the model more accurately assigned risk probabilities, improving discrimination between patients with good versus poor prognoses compared to the original WIFI, SINBAD, or UTWCS systems. Table presents performance metrics (accuracy, F1 score, precision, recall, specificity and AUC) for all systems and their modified versions, highlighting the improvements achieved through targeted feature modifications. 4 Discussion Our analysis provides critical insights into the performance of various wound classification systems, particularly in the context of prognostic prediction. The univariate models assessed in our study demonstrated limited efficacy across all classification systems, reinforcing the notion that relying solely on traditional scoring methods may be insufficient for accurate clinical decision‐making. This highlights the necessity of validating wound classification systems in diverse settings with varying demographic and clinical characteristics, as each system may lack the power to effectively identify cases with poor prognosis, especially given the differences in facility levels and specialised resources. The challenges faced by different countries due to varying conditions can significantly impact the effectiveness capacity of classification systems. Factors such as inadequate training and supervision of staff in correctly classifying wounds and managing them appropriately, as well as the lack of periodic calibration of diagnostic tools, can hinder performance. Furthermore, socio‐economic factors, such as delays in patients' time to first visit, extended waiting times for specialised services in the public sector, high costs associated with private sector care and insufficient or lacking insurance coverage, underscore the urgent need for prognostic tools tailored to specific settings. IWGDF has emphasised the importance of validating these tools before recommending their implementation for effective communication among healthcare staff [ ]. appropriately, as well as the lack of periodic calibration of diagnostic tools, can hinder performance. Furthermore, socio‐economic factors, such as delays in patients' time to first visit, extended waiting times for specialised services in the public sector, high costs associated with private sector care and insufficient or lacking insurance coverage, underscore the urgent need for prognostic tools tailored to specific settings. IWGDF has emphasised the importance of validating these tools before recommending their implementation for effective communication among healthcare staff [ ]. However, the IWGDF guidelines emphasise that none of the currently available classification systems should be used to provide individual patient outcome prognosis. In line with these recommendations, the objective of this study was not to generate individual‐level prognostic predictions for clinical decision‐making. Instead, we evaluated the comparative discriminative performance at the population level of commonly used DFU classification systems for identifying patients at higher risk of non‐healing in an outpatient cohort, using statistical and machine learning approaches. Based on the results of our study, both the SINBAD and UTWCS classification systems outperformed other classification systems, particularly the WIFI system, in predicting poor prognostic outcomes. In a study similar to ours in Scotland [ ], two classification tools, UTWCS and SINBAD, were compared, concluding that they both performed similarly in predicting poor prognosis outcomes. Furthermore, a study in Manchester [ ] found that the UTWCS tool exhibited better performance than the Wagner classification. In contrast, other studies [ , , ], indicated that the WIFI system outperformed the others in predicting healing time and provided superior information regarding amputation risk. Additionally, in a study [ ], three tools—PEDIS, SINBAD and Wagner—were compared, revealing that PEDIS demonstrated superior diagnostic power compared to the other two tools. Our results suggest that the relatively weaker performance of the WIFI system can be attributed to two main factors. First, the wound component in the WIFI system is primarily designed for extensive or gangrenous wounds, which were less prevalent in the outpatient clinic setting of this study. Second, the system's effectiveness was limited by the unavailability of specialised equipment, such as transcutaneous oxygen pressure and toe blood pressure measurements, which are essential for accurately assessing ischemia. Moreover, reliance on ABI for ischemia categorization introduced limitations, particularly as many diabetic patients had ABI values > 1.3 due to arterial calcification, masking true ischemia [ ]. Furthermore, our ABI device designated values < 0.5 as E1, limiting precision in assessing varying degrees of ischemia in patients with values below 0.5. Our findings align with recent IWGDF recommendations advocating for classification systems that do not necessitate specialised equipment, such as toe pressure and TcPO2 measurements. Following these recommendations, the SINBAD system stands out as a straightforward and efficient system, requiring only a clinical examination. It provides crucial information for triage by healthcare professionals, facilitating effective communication regarding wound characteristics. We also proposed modifications to existing classification systems, which yielded promising results. Specifically, in the WIFI system, revising the component related to the wound assessment markedly enhanced the system's predictive capabilities for poor outcomes. The modification of the wound component to a simpler depth classification—designating wounds as 1 for Skin, 2 for Muscle and 3 for Tendon, Joint and Bone—allowed for clearer categorization. As a result, sensitivity improved from 70.7% in the original model to 77.6%, surpassing the performance of all existing systems. The F1 scores and precision metrics also ranked highly, indicating that the modified system was well‐suited for routine outpatient care settings, which typically encounter fewer complex wounds, and can improve feasibility for the healthcare providers operating at these primary care levels and not limit its utility in specialised hospitals and tertiary care centers. In the present study, peripheral neuropathy was not significantly associated with wound healing outcomes. This finding appears to differ from several previous studies, which identified neuropathy as an independent predictor of non‐healing [ , , , ]. However, an important explanation lies in the very high prevalence of neuropathy in our cohort (95.3%), resulting in limited variability and reduced statistical power to detect its independent effect. From a pathophysiological perspective, neuropathy is widely recognised as a key factor in the development of diabetic foot ulcers, primarily through loss of protective sensation, foot deformity, altered pressure distribution, and skin breakdown [ , , , ]. Its role in impairing wound healing after ulcer formation, however, is less consistent in the literature. Several studies suggest that neuropathy primarily acts upstream by facilitating ulcer occurrence, whereas peripheral arterial disease and infection play more direct roles in delayed healing and tissue loss. Although some human studies and animal models suggest that neuropathy may adversely affect wound healing through vascular, metabolic, and inflammatory mechanisms, clinical evidence remains heterogeneous [ , ]. 4.1 Our Study Had Several Limitations In our study, ABI is used to assess ischemia in

deformity, altered pressure distribution, and skin breakdown [ , , , ]. Its role in impairing wound healing after ulcer formation, however, is less consistent in the literature. Several studies suggest that neuropathy primarily acts upstream by facilitating ulcer occurrence, whereas peripheral arterial disease and infection play more direct roles in delayed healing and tissue loss. Although some human studies and animal models suggest that neuropathy may adversely affect wound healing through vascular, metabolic, and inflammatory mechanisms, clinical evidence remains heterogeneous [ , ]. 4.1 Our Study Had Several Limitations In our study, ABI is used to assess ischemia in the WIFI classification system, which ABI has known limitations in diabetes due to medial arterial calcification, which can lead to falsely elevated values (> 1.3) and misclassification of ischemia as normal. This limitation may partially explain the weaker performance of ischemia‐dependent systems such as WIFI in this study. The WIFI classification requires more detailed ischemia assessment, ideally including toe pressure or transcutaneous oxygen measurements. However, such measurements were not available in our setting. Since most wound centers in our setting lacked these tools, as a result, ischemia severity may have been underestimated, reducing the predictive performance of WIFI. This limitation underscores the need for classification systems that align with the structural constraints of such facilities. Also, the apparent inconsistency in the prognostic significance of PAD across classification systems likely reflects differences in ischemia assessment rather than true disagreement. Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) was defined differently across the classification systems included in this study, reflecting their original conceptual frameworks. In the DiaFORA classification, perfusion status represents severe ischemia and was determined based on clinical assessment of peripheral pulses (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries). The presence of ≤ 1 palpable pedal pulse was defined as PAD. In contrast, other classification systems primarily defined PAD based on ankle–brachial index (ABI) measurements, with values < 0.9 or > 1.3, or absence of palpable pulses considered abnormal. Another limitation is some laboratory predictors had missing values; we addressed this issue using multiple imputation methods, but residual bias cannot be excluded. Third, class imbalance is a common challenge in prognostic studies of diabetic foot ulcers. Although resampling techniques such as oversampling, undersampling and SMOTE are frequently recommended, their effectiveness depends on data structure and sample size. In our study, resampling approaches did not improve test‐set performance and occasionally degraded model generalisation. The lack of performance improvement with SMOTE may be explained by the moderate degree of imbalance, the relatively limited number of non‐healed cases and the high dimensionality and clinical heterogeneity of the predictor space. In such settings, synthetic samples may not adequately capture clinically meaningful patterns and can introduce noise, leading to reduced generalisation performance. Similar observations have been reported in medical prediction studies with structured clinical data. Finally, although information on medications was collected, data on the specific time frame and duration of use were not available, limiting our ability to fully assess their potential impact on outcomes. In this study we didn't assess calibration to develop probabilistic risk scores or treatment thresholds to guide clinical decisions, because our primary goal was to compare the predictive accuracy of different wound classification systems focusing on metrics derived from predicted class labels, including F1 score, sensitivity, specificity and AUC. Additionally, calibration in small datasets poses challenges. Techniques such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression, or cross‐validated calibration require further data splitting, which can reduce the effective sample size, worsen overfitting, or yield unstable calibration curves. Class imbalance can further complicate calibration assessment. In our study, we proposed modifications to the existing classification systems aimed at improving their performance and enhancing the feasibility of these systems in outpatient services. Future research is essential to validate these modified systems in larger, multicenter studies focused on determining their generalizability and effectiveness in improving patient outcomes. 5 Conclusion In our outpatient sample, the SINBAD and UTWCS classification systems demonstrated the strongest performance when incorporated into predictive models, consistently achieving higher sensitivity and F1 scores compared with other systems. Our proposed modification of the wound component in the WIFI system also improved its performance, suggesting potential applicability for outpatient services and less specialised clinical settings. chunks.content: Introduction Infected bone defects are common and serious complications following trauma, osteomyelitis, and revision surgeries, particularly when large bone defects of the limbs are accompanied by soft tissue damage [ ]. These bone defects often lead to recurrent infections due to the loss of mechanical support, persistent infection, and insufficient soft tissue coverage [ ]. Traditional treatments such as autologous bone grafting, the Masquelet technique, and Ilizarov bone transport face challenges such as long treatment cycles, a high incidence of complications (with infection recurrence rates ranging from 15% to 30%), and limited functional recovery [ – ]. In recent years, 3D-printed customized titanium alloy prostheses have provided a new direction for bone defect reconstruction after infection control, thanks to their advantages in precise anatomical matching, immediate mechanical stability, and microporous structure that promotes bone ingrowth [ , ]. The clinical application of 3D-printed microporous titanium in orthopedics initially began with the repair and reconstruction after bone tumor resection and limb-salvage surgeries, achieving favorable results [ ]. In osteomyelitis treatment, given the complexity and high cost of traditional Masquelet and Ilizarov bone transport techniques, personalized 3D printing technology can promote bone-prosthesis interface integration and bone ingrowth through porosity, while maintaining good mechanical support [ ]. Furthermore, soft tissue defects associated with complex cases remain a key factor limiting their effectiveness. The lack of well-vascularized soft tissue coverage significantly increases the risk of prosthesis exposure and recurrent infection [ ]. For the repair of soft tissue defects of varying degrees, free flap techniques (such as the anterolateral thigh free flap) can effectively reduce dead space, promote wound healing, and reduce the risk of deep infection by providing well-vascularized tissue coverage [ , ]. Current research on the treatment of infected bone defects primarily focuses on single treatment strategies, such as prosthesis implantation or local pedicled flap repair. For example, Liu et al. [ ] reported on the use of 3D-printed microporous titanium implants for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis, with 6 out of 8 patients achieving good bone integration. We also reported the use of single microporous titanium prosthesis implantation for treating 18 patients with infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis, with 17 patients (94.4%) achieving good healing [ ]. Previously, in 2022, we first reported the preliminary efficacy of free/local flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium for treating 6 cases of lower limb infected bone defects with soft tissue loss, with 5 patients achieving good wound healing (83.3%) [ ]. Additionally, Chen et al. [ ] used local transposition flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium to treat 13 patients with femoral bone defects following osteomyelitis, achieving good bone integration and wound healing in 7 cases during follow-up. However, the personalized harvesting of free flaps and the advantages of covering large soft tissue defects are not addressed in existing studies. On the other hand, current research is limited to lower limb cases, with a lack of evidence for the efficacy in upper limb infected bone defects. Importantly, these clinical efficacy and safety data have not been validated in large-scale studies. The biomechanical performance of the 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis has been systematically evaluated in our previous study using integrated biomechanical testing and finite element analysis, which demonstrated sufficient load-bearing capacity, favorable stress distribution, and resistance to fatigue failure [ ]. Building on this biomechanical foundation, we conducted the largest single-center retrospective cohort study to date to evaluate the clinical safety and effectiveness of a staged reconstructive strategy incorporating personalized 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses for infected bone defects. This strategy integrates individualized prosthesis implantation with free flap reconstruction when required, allowing its application to infected bone defects with varying degrees of soft tissue involvement at different anatomical locations in the limbs (Fig. ). In addition to assessing overall clinical outcomes, we explored risk factors associated with postoperative complications. Patients were further stratified into subgroups according to the presence or absence of significant soft tissue defects, namely a single prosthesis group and a combined free flap group. Rather than aiming to compare these subgroups for superiority, subgroup analyses were performed to characterize clinical features and recovery trajectories across different tiers of reconstructive complexity, thereby evaluating the applicability and universality of the staged treatment protocol. The staged approach consisted of: (1) infection control with or without individualized free flap coverage based on soft tissue requirements; and (2) definitive bone reconstruction using a customized 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis. Our institution specializes in the treatment of infected bone defects caused by various factors and has extensive experience in limb repair and reconstruction. After approval from the institutional ethics review board (2019-018-02), we conducted a retrospective data collection and analysis of a series of patients who underwent microporous titanium implant treatment from January 2019 to January

treatment protocol. Materials and methods Study design This is a retrospective study. Our institution specializes in the treatment of infected bone defects caused by various factors and has extensive experience in limb repair and reconstruction. After approval from the institutional ethics review board (2019-018-02), we conducted a retrospective data collection and analysis of a series of patients who underwent microporous titanium implant treatment from January 2019 to January 2025. This cohort study has been reported in line with the STROCSS guidelines [ , ]. Patient selection The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) For bone defect characteristics, patients with infected nonunion or traumatic bone defects in the limbs (including tibia, femur, humerus, radius, carpal bones, metacarpal bones, and metatarsal bones, etc.) where the bone defect length after debridement could not be repaired by traditional autologous or artificial bone grafts (confirmed by imaging measurements and 3D CT reconstruction); (2) Patients with concomitant soft tissue defects that could not be closed by direct suturing or skin grafting (evaluated by wound measurement software or intraoperative sterile film method); (3) Postoperative follow-up ≥ 3 months with complete imaging (X-ray/CT) and laboratory data. Additionally, the study excluded the following: (1) Severe uncontrolled underlying diseases (such as uncontrolled diabetes: HbA1c > 8%, heart failure grade III-IV, cirrhosis Child-Pugh class C) (2), Long-term use of immunosuppressants or corticosteroids (prednisone ≥ 10 mg/d, continuous use for > 3 months); (3) Tumor-related bone destruction (primary bone tumors or metastatic tumors), radiation-induced bone necrosis, congenital skeletal deformities; (4) Loss to follow-up or missing critical data (imaging, functional scores). All surgeries were performed by the same senior surgeon to reduce heterogeneity in the procedure. Surgical technique and postoperative rehabilitation This study employed a two-stage surgical approach to treat complex infected bone defects. Prior to the second surgery, a 3D CT scan was used to assess the morphology of the bone defect and the extent of soft tissue involvement, after which an individualized 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis was custom-designed (pore diameter 700–750 μm, porosity 65–75%). The first-stage surgery involved thorough debridement, removal of necrotic bone and soft tissue, and the implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement (2 g vancomycin/40 g bone cement). Simultaneously, a free anterolateral thigh flap was used to repair the concomitant soft tissue defect in 25 cases. Postoperatively, antibiotic treatment based on bacterial culture results was administered until the infection was completely controlled (CRP, ESR, and white blood cell counts normalized for two consecutive tests). In the second-stage surgery, the induced membrane was preserved, bone cement was removed, and the pre-designed microporous titanium prosthesis was implanted (secured by intramedullary protrusion anchor and titanium plate fixation). The surface of the prosthesis was coated with vancomycin sulfate calcium. Regardless of whether the procedure involved a single implantation or a combined free flap repair, all patients received standardized nursing and rehabilitation. Detailed information regarding staged surgery and postoperative rehabilitation can be found in Supplemental Material 1, including first-stage surgery, postoperative management, design and manufacturing of 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis, and second-stage surgery and postoperative rehabilitation. Data collection and outcome measures Outpatient follow-up and data collection were performed at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, with annual reviews thereafter. All follow-up data were collected and organized by research assistants, and electronic medical records were reviewed, including case files, surgical details, laboratory, and imaging data. The baseline data obtained for patients included age, gender, and medical history; primary characteristics included etiology (traumatic or non-traumatic) of the bone defect, location, length, soft tissue defect area, flap type, and bacterial culture results. Laboratory and imaging assessments (X-ray and CT) were performed preoperatively and at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively, with subsequent annual checks. Visual analogue scale (VAS) scores [ ] were recorded at each follow-up. CRP and ESR were measured at each follow-up time point, and infection control was considered achieved if the values normalized for two consecutive tests (CRP < 10 mg/L, ESR < 20 mm/h). Additionally, implant integration and stability were evaluated using X-ray and CT examinations. Successful implant integration was defined by fulfillment of all of the following criteria: (1) progressive trabecular bone formation at the bone–prosthesis interface; (2) absence of progressive radiolucent lines greater than 2 mm; and (3) absence of implant migration, loosening, or mechanical failure. Failure to meet any one of these criteria was classified as poor implant integration. For lower limb cases, postoperative functional recovery was assessed using the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS) [ ], recording the postoperative standing time, walking time with crutches, and time to full weight-bearing. Infection eradication was assessed based on a comprehensive evaluation combining clinical, laboratory, and radiological

Failure to meet any one of these criteria was classified as poor implant integration. For lower limb cases, postoperative functional recovery was assessed using the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS) [ ], recording the postoperative standing time, walking time with crutches, and time to full weight-bearing. Infection eradication was assessed based on a comprehensive evaluation combining clinical, laboratory, and radiological criteria. Clinical signs included the absence of sinus tract, persistent drainage, local erythema, swelling, or pain. Additionally, pre-defined complications included wound recurrent infection, flap necrosis, poor wound healing, prosthesis-related infections, prosthesis-related fractures, implant fractures, and non-union. Statistical analysis Data analysis was performed using IBM SPSS (version 29.0). For baseline data, continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) and categorical variables were expressed as frequency (percentage). Differences in LEFS and VAS scores before and after surgery were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Predefined complications (such as recurrent infection, prosthesis fracture, etc.) were treated as binary outcome variables. Univariate logistic regression was performed to assess the relationship between patients’ baseline characteristics (age, gender, bone defect length, etc.) and surgical features (flap repair, bacterial type, etc.). Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics From February 2019 to January 2025, 82 patients with osteomyelitis caused by trauma or non-trauma underwent staged surgeries. All patients signed an informed consent form for surgery. Two patients were excluded because they did not undergo the second-stage surgery after the first debridement and vancomycin-loaded implant. In the end, 80 patients met the eligibility criteria and were included in the analysis. Among these, 54 were male (67.5%) and 26 were female (32.5%), with an average age of 47.5 ± 9.3 years, an average BMI of 26.6 ± 2.9 kg/m², and an average follow-up time of 40.8 ± 14.8 months. The majority of infected bone defects were traumatic (52 cases, 65%). There were 24 patients with a history of hypertension, 10 with a history of diabetes, and 4 with both hypertension and diabetes. The median bone defect length was 11.4 cm (range 3.8–32.0 cm), and the soft tissue defect area ranged from approximately 5.0 × 8.0 cm to 33 × 10 cm (Table ). None of the 80 patients lost to follow-up at the last visit. Among the 55 cases in the single microporous titanium implant group, 37 were male (69.1%) and 18 were female (30.9%), with an average age of 47.0 ± 7.8 years and an average follow-up time of 42.8 ± 12.3 months. The range of soft tissue defect area was approximately 5.0 cm × 8.0 cm to 33 cm × 10 cm. The median bone defect length was 10.5 cm (range 3.5–28.0 cm), including 32 cases of tibial bone defects, 11 cases of femoral bone defects, 5 cases of humeral bone defects, 4 cases of radial bone defects, and 3 cases of combined carpal and metacarpal bone defects. In the free flap combined group, there were 25 cases, with 17 males (68.0%) and 8 females (32.0%), with an average age of 48.5 ± 12.1 years and an average follow-up time of 36.4 ± 15.5 months. The median bone defect length was 12.0 cm (range 3.8–32.0 cm), including 3 cases with extensive dorsal foot soft tissue defects accompanied by large segments of metatarsal bone defects, 19 cases with lower leg soft tissue defects accompanied by large segments of tibial bone defects, and 3 cases of hand and forearm soft tissue defects combined with metacarpal and carpal bone defects. The bacterial culture results from the first-stage surgery showed that among the 25 patients in the free flap combined group, Gram-positive (G⁺) infections accounted for 76% (19/25), primarily Staphylococcus aureus (14/25) and Staphylococcus epidermidis (5/25). Gram-negative (G⁻) infections accounted for 16% (4/25), all due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Mixed infections ( Staphylococcus aureus + Pseudomonas aeruginosa ) accounted for 8% (2/25). For the 55 cases in the single microporous titanium implant group, G⁺ infections accounted for 78.2% (43/55), with Staphylococcus aureus being the predominant pathogen (65.5%, 36/55), followed by coagulase-negative staphylococci ( Staphylococcus epidermidis in 7 cases). G⁻ infections accounted for 14.5% (8/55), including Pseudomonas aeruginosa (4/9) and Escherichia coli (4/9). Mixed infections accounted for 7.3% (4/55), with Staphylococcus aureus + Pseudomonas aeruginosa in 3 cases, and Staphylococcus aureus + Escherichia coli in 1 case. Overall clinical efficacy The average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.2 ± 1.4, which decreased to 1.6 ± 0.7 at 12 months postoperatively. The VAS score at the last follow-up was 1.2 ± 0.4 (Table ).

Mixed infections accounted for 7.3% (4/55), with Staphylococcus aureus + Pseudomonas aeruginosa in 3 cases, and Staphylococcus aureus + Escherichia coli in 1 case. Overall clinical efficacy The average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.2 ± 1.4, which decreased to 1.6 ± 0.7 at 12 months postoperatively. The VAS score at the last follow-up was 1.2 ± 0.4 (Table ). At each postoperative follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up), VAS scores significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001). For lower limb cases ( N = 65), the average baseline LEFS score preoperatively was 28.5 ± 5.8, with significant improvements in the LEFS score at each follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up) ( p < 0.0001). The average time to first standing for lower limb patients was 2.1 ± 0.5 months, the average time to first walking with crutches was 3.8 ± 1.1 months, and the average time to full weight-bearing was 5.3 ± 0.9 months. Based on the implant integration by X-ray and CT examinations, the number of cases rated as “Excellent” and “Poor” were 69 (86.3%) and 11 (13.7%), respectively. The representative case is shown in Fig. . Subgroup analysis In the single microporous titanium implant group ( N = 55), the average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.0 ± 1.5. At each follow-up time point, VAS scores significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001; Fig. ). For lower limb cases ( N = 43), the average baseline LEFS score preoperatively was 29.2 ± 5.2, with significantly higher scores observed at each follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up) ( p < 0.0001). The average time to first standing for lower limb patients was 2.0 ± 0.6 months, the average time to first walking with crutches was 3.5 ± 1.1 months, and the average time to full weight-bearing was 5.1 ± 0.7 months. Based on the implant integration by X-ray and CT examinations, the number of cases rated as “Excellent” and “Poor” were 50 (90.9%) and 5 (9.1%), respectively. For the free flap combined group ( N = 25), the average baseline VAS score preoperatively was 7.6 ± 1.2. At each follow-up time point, VAS scores significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001; Fig. ). For lower limb cases ( N = 22), the average baseline LEFS score preoperatively was 27.1 ± 6.7, with significantly higher scores observed at each follow-up time point (3 months, 6 months, 12 months, and the last follow-up) ( p < 0.0001). The average time to first standing for lower limb patients was 2.3 ± 0.5 months, the average time to first walking with crutches was 4.2 ± 1.2 months, and the average time to full weight-bearing was 5.8 ± 1.1 months. For implant integration, the number of cases rated as “Excellent” and “Poor” were 19 (76%) and 6 (24%), respectively. Complications A total of 8 complications occurred during the postoperative follow-up period among 80 patients, resulting in an overall complication rate of 10% (Table ). The complications were categorized as recurrent infections and prosthesis fractures, occurring at an average of 7.5 ± 3.6 months postoperatively. Among these, recurrent infection was the most common complication (7.5%), occurring at an average of 5.8 ± 3.1 months postoperatively. Prosthesis fracture occurred in 2.5% of cases, with an average onset at 11.5 months postoperatively. Notably, the tibia was the most common site of complications, accounting for 50% of all complications. Specifically, in the single 3D-printed microporous titanium prosthesis group, two patients experienced recurrent tibial infections at 6 and 11 months postoperatively. After debridement, vancomycin-loaded bone cement was implanted, and both patients resumed walking at 6- and 8-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent infection at 5 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 6 months post second-stage surgery. Another patient in the same group experienced a femoral prosthesis fracture at 13 months postoperatively, which was followed by prosthesis removal and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored 7 months after the second-stage surgery. In the free flap combined treatment group, two diabetic patients developed foot wound infections at 3 and 4 months postoperatively. Both patients underwent prosthesis removal and replacement with vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored at 5- and 7-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent tibial infection at 8 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 4 months after the second-stage surgery. Another patient had a tibial

13 months postoperatively, which was followed by prosthesis removal and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored 7 months after the second-stage surgery. In the free flap combined treatment group, two diabetic patients developed foot wound infections at 3 and 4 months postoperatively. Both patients underwent prosthesis removal and replacement with vancomycin-loaded bone cement, with walking restored at 5- and 7-months post second-stage surgery, respectively. One patient developed a recurrent tibial infection at 8 months postoperatively, and after debridement and implantation of vancomycin-loaded bone cement, walking was restored 4 months after the second-stage surgery. Another patient had a tibial fixation prosthesis screw fracture at 10 months postoperatively. After revision surgery, walking was restored 5 months later, with no recurrence of infection observed. Risk factors of complications Exploratory risk factor analysis ( Table ) showed that diabetes mellitus was associated with a higher occurrence of postoperative complications in both univariate logistic regression (OR = 11; p = 0.004) and Fisher’s exact test ( p = 0.007). The increased risk of recurrent infection was associated with a history of diabetes (OR = 9.571; p = 0.013) and bacterial culture results showing mixed infection (OR = 8.75; p = 0.031). No significant associations were observed between other baseline characteristics and prosthesis-related mechanical failure. However, given the small number of events, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Discussion In this study, the most significant finding was that 90% of patients did not experience recurrence after receiving either single microporous titanium implantation or combined free flap treatment, with an average follow-up of 40.8 months. The postoperative 1-year VAS score significantly decreased from 7.2 ± 1.4 to 1.6 ± 0.7 ( p < 0.0001), and the LEFS score for the lower limbs increased from 28.5 ± 5.8 to a median score of 59.0 ( p < 0.0001). The implant integration was rated as “Excellent” in 86.3% of cases. Additionally, we found that a history of diabetes and mixed bacterial infections may be important risk factors for recurrent infections. Over the past few decades, both the Masquelet and Ilizarov techniques have been clinically applied as important treatment options for infected bone defects [ , ]. However, the effectiveness of these methods may be compromised by complications such as pin tract infections, donor site infections, non-union, mechanical issues, or even recurrent fractures [ , ]. Many patients are unable to bear weight during the early postoperative recovery period. For example, a previous clinical efficacy comparison analysis showed that the average fixation time for the Masquelet and Ilizarov groups was 10.15 months and 17.21 months, respectively, with the Masquelet group demonstrating better functional outcomes [ ]. For cases without soft tissue defects, our study showed a treatment success rate of 92.7% (51/55) in the single microporous titanium prosthesis implantation group, with complete weight-bearing achieved on average after 5.0 ± 0.7 months. Pain was significantly relieved at 3 months postoperatively and continued to improve until the last follow-up. This may be attributed to the protective role of complete soft tissue coverage on the prosthesis, preventing microbial colonization and mechanical stress concentration. For cases with soft tissue defects, despite more complex bone and soft tissue defects and reliance on microsurgical techniques for free flap coverage, a treatment success rate of 84.0% (21/25) was still achieved, which is consistent with previously reported success rates (82.3–96.5%) [ , ]. Postoperative pain and lower limb function continued to improve at 3 months and beyond, with full weight-bearing achieved at 5.8 ± 1.1 months. The core advantage of free flap combined reconstruction for infected bone defects with soft tissue loss lies in the vascular support provided by the free flap, which may further influence bone healing outcomes. Given the fundamental differences in baseline disease severity and soft tissue involvement between patients treated with single prosthesis implantation and those requiring combined free flap reconstruction, these subgroups were analyzed as distinct cohorts representing different tiers of reconstructive complexity rather than being directly compared for treatment superiority. Personalized free flap The results of this study demonstrate certain advantages over traditional treatment methods, such as the Masquelet technique. Chen et al. [ ] reported in a previous clinical study that the combination of 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation and the Masquelet technique for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis achieved a treatment success rate of 76.9% (10/13). They then preliminarily explored the efficacy of local pedicled flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation for treating tibial infected bone defects, with a treatment success rate of less than 60% (53.8%, 7/13 cases) [ ]. Notably, the incidence of flap-related complications in that study was 30.8%, which may have been due to poor blood supply and excessive tension at the flap margins. In contrast, we did not observe any cases of free flap transplantation failure or related complications. The

and the Masquelet technique for treating infected bone defects caused by osteomyelitis achieved a treatment success rate of 76.9% (10/13). They then preliminarily explored the efficacy of local pedicled flaps combined with 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation for treating tibial infected bone defects, with a treatment success rate of less than 60% (53.8%, 7/13 cases) [ ]. Notably, the incidence of flap-related complications in that study was 30.8%, which may have been due to poor blood supply and excessive tension at the flap margins. In contrast, we did not observe any cases of free flap transplantation failure or related complications. The second-stage prosthesis implantation surgery was performed on average 4.8 ± 1.4 months after the first-stage free flap transplantation surgery. Innovatively, we used a personalized free flap (free anterolateral thigh flap) for repairing complex and large soft tissue defects, while also expanding the bone defect area from lower limb to limb-wide infected bone defects. By implementing precise infection control strategies (vancomycin-loaded bone cement release + pathogen-guided antibiotic therapy), we further enhanced the therapeutic efficacy, and the study preliminarily verified the feasibility of staged treatment (first-stage infection control combined with flap repair of soft tissue defects, second-stage mechanical reconstruction) for complex infected bone defects. Although the anterolateral thigh flap was the preferred option in the present series, alternative free flaps may be indicated depending on the characteristics of the defect and patient-related factors. The latissimus dorsi flap provides a large volume of well-vascularized tissue and is suitable for extensive soft tissue defects [ ]. The radial forearm flap offers thin and pliable coverage for smaller defects requiring contour precision [ ]. The gracilis flap may be considered for moderate-sized defects when a shorter operative time and limited donor-site morbidity are desired [ ]. In selected cases, a free fibular flap can simultaneously address segmental bone loss and soft tissue defects, although its use may be limited in the setting of infection or compromised recipient vessels [ ]. Therefore, free flap selection should be individualized based on defect size, location, infection status, and reconstructive goals. Diabetes and recurrent infections Regarding postoperative complications, the overall complication rate was 10% (8/80), with recurrent infection (7.5%) and prosthesis and screw mechanical fractures (2.5%) being the most common. Among them, two diabetic patients with extensive dorsal foot soft tissue defects accompanied by large metatarsal bone defects both experienced recurrent infections postoperatively, and one diabetic patient had a recurrent tibial infection. Univariate logistic regression analysis showed that a history of diabetes was significantly associated with a higher risk of any complications and recurrent infection ( p < 0.05), which drew our attention to diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Previous studies have shown that in diabetic patients, the significant changes in ischemia and neuropathy are primarily in the foot, which greatly increases the risk of foot bone infection [ , ]. In response, our experience suggests that preoperative strict control of HbA1c (≤ 7.5%) and serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L should be prioritized. After microporous titanium implantation, we extended the antibiotic regimen to 8 weeks (instead of the usual 2 weeks) and used dynamic follow-up with infection markers to monitor recurrent infections. For the 3 cases of recurrent infection in diabetic patients, the medical team conducted detailed discussions and analyses, discovering that patients had not received standardized foot care after discharge, which may have contributed to the infection recurrence. Additionally, all three patients had varying degrees of peripheral vascular disease, which posed a challenge to flap survival and the growth environment. Therefore, we recommend that before surgical treatment of diabetic osteomyelitis patients, classification according to guidelines (high risk, low risk, or moderate risk), such as the DFU prevention and management guidelines published by the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) [ ], should be conducted to facilitate targeted, stratified treatment. Diabetes is known to impair immune function, microcirculation, and wound healing, which may contribute to persistent or recurrent infection [ ]. In our clinical practice, diabetes was not considered a contraindication to microporous titanium implantation or free flap reconstruction; however, these patients were managed as a high-risk subgroup. Management strategies included strict preoperative glycemic control, optimization of nutritional and metabolic status, thorough and staged debridement when necessary, and close postoperative surveillance for early signs of infection recurrence [ , ]. Multidisciplinary collaboration with endocrinologists and infected disease specialists was routinely employed. These measures may help mitigate infection-related risks in diabetic patients, although careful patient selection and individualized treatment planning remain essential. Moreover, Metaoy et al. [ ] found that local use of antibiotic-loaded implants can increase the eradication rate of infection in diabetic foot osteomyelitis and may further reduce amputation and mortality rates. Another meta-analysis showed that diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients treated with local antibiotic delivery systems had significantly higher healing rates compared to the control group [ ].

These measures may help mitigate infection-related risks in diabetic patients, although careful patient selection and individualized treatment planning remain essential. Moreover, Metaoy et al. [ ] found that local use of antibiotic-loaded implants can increase the eradication rate of infection in diabetic foot osteomyelitis and may further reduce amputation and mortality rates. Another meta-analysis showed that diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients treated with local antibiotic delivery systems had significantly higher healing rates compared to the control group [ ]. In this regard, developing a local antibiotic delivery system on the surface of microporous titanium or modifying it for controlled drug release could be an effective strategy for treating diabetic foot infected bone defects. Nevertheless, the retrospective design of this study inevitably introduces the risk of selection bias and limits the ability to draw causal inferences. In contrast, a prospective study design would enable predefined inclusion criteria, standardized data collection, and uniform follow-up protocols, thereby improving data completeness and internal validity. Future prospective studies or registries are therefore warranted to further validate the clinical effectiveness and safety of 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses in the management of infected bone defects. Additionally, from a clinical applicability perspective, several practical factors merit consideration, including cost, operative duration, and prosthesis manufacturing time. Patient-specific 3D-printed titanium prostheses generally involve higher upfront costs and require a manufacturing period for design and printing [ , ]. However, these factors may be balanced by potential clinical advantages, such as reduced need for staged reconstruction, earlier weight-bearing, and avoidance of prolonged external fixation in selected cases. Operative duration is primarily influenced by the extent of bone and soft tissue defects and the need for combined free flap reconstruction, rather than by prosthesis implantation alone. Future studies incorporating standardized cost-effectiveness and workflow analyses are needed to further define the role of this technique in routine clinical practice. Limitations This study has several limitations: (1) The retrospective design may introduce recall bias, and the lack of a control group (such as comparisons with traditional Masquelet or Ilizarov technique) may lead to selection bias. Future studies should include prospective randomized controlled trials to verify long-term efficacy while expanding the sample size; (2) The cases in this study are still concentrated in the early to mid-term follow-up, lacking long-term follow-up data beyond 10 years, which makes it difficult to assess prosthesis wear and the risk of late loosening; (3) A limitation of this study is the absence of a validated upper-extremity functional outcome measure, such as the DASH or QuickDASH questionnaire. This was primarily due to the very small number of upper-extremity cases in the combined free flap group ( n = 3), which would have rendered meaningful statistical analysis underpowered and potentially misleading. Future prospective studies with larger, multi-center cohorts are needed to allow balanced anatomical representation and comprehensive limb-specific functional evaluation (4). Risk factor exploration was based on univariate logistic regression only. Given the small number of events, multivariable modeling was not performed to avoid overfitting. Future studies with larger event numbers should apply multivariable regression to better control for confounding. Despite these limitations, this study represents the largest cohort of patients to date who underwent 3D-printed microporous titanium implantation or combined free flap repair and reconstruction for infected bone defects of the limbs, with or without soft tissue defects. The average follow-up of 40.8 months provides preliminary evidence for the feasibility and universality of personalized customization and staged treatment. In conclusion, 3D-printed microporous titanium prostheses (either alone or combined with free flaps) provide a reliable staged solution for limb infected bone defects. Throughout the follow-up period (≥ 3 months), both the single microporous titanium group and the free flap combined group maintained continuous improvements in pain relief and lower limb function. However, larger-sample and longer-term randomized controlled trials are still required in the future to validate the feasibility and safety of this surgical approach. documents.title: IWGDF Guideline on Classification of Diabetic Foot Ulcers

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are among the most serious chronic complications of diabetes, with a lifetime incidence of up to 34% ( ) and an increasingly younger affected population. DFUs arise from the interplay of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), and impaired immune function, typically presenting as skin breakdown, infection, or tissue necrosis that may extend to bone or joints. These lesions markedly increase the risk of amputation—with reported rates up to 33%—and lead to disability in approximately 20% of patients ( , ), representing a major public health challenge. Once a DFU becomes infected, the resulting diabetic foot infection (DFI) usually begins with microbial colonization following disruption of the skin barrier and progresses under conditions of hyperglycemia, microvascular dysfunction, and impaired neutrophil activity ( ). Notably, the clinical manifestations of DFI may be masked by neuropathy, PAD, or immunosuppression; some patients develop deep tissue involvement or osteomyelitis without typical signs of inflammation ( , ). Thus, infection assessment should not rely solely on culture results but must integrate wound characteristics, systemic symptoms, and imaging evidence ( ). The severity of DFI is closely related to its anatomical spread. The foot’s fascial compartments facilitate proximal extension of infection along tendons and fascial planes. When inflammatory pressure increases within these closed spaces, ischemic necrosis may ensue, accelerating disease progression ( , ). Patients with chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled diabetes, or recurrent ulcers are at even higher risk for necrotizing or systemic infections ( ). Although many infections begin superficially, without timely intervention, they may rapidly invade deeper soft tissues, joints, or bone, posing a serious threat to limb and life ( ). Current international guidelines recommend staging DFIs based on infection extent, depth, and systemic involvement, and tailoring treatment accordingly—including antimicrobial therapy, debridement, revascularization, and multidisciplinary management ( ). However, large-scale, stratified clinical evidence on stage-based treatment of infected DFUs remains limited in China. To address this gap, we retrospectively analyzed 300 patients with DFU-associated infections using the IWGDF/IDSA classification system ( , ) to stratify infection severity, guide individualized treatment, and evaluate clinical outcomes. This study aims to provide evidence for standardized, stepwise management of DFIs, optimize treatment pathways, reduce amputation rates, and improve patient prognosis. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design This was a single-center, retrospective observational cohort study. The study aimed to systematically evaluate the real-world application, microbiological characteristics, treatment response, and long-term clinical outcomes of a stage-based treatment strategy guided by the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot/Infectious Diseases Society of America (IWGDF/IDSA) clinical classification system in patients with diabetic foot infection (DFI). The study protocol was designed and conducted in strict accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and received formal approval from the hospital’s Institutional Review Board prior to initiation (Approval No. 2019–701). As this study involved secondary analysis of existing, anonymized clinical data without new interventions, and all data collection and processing adhered to strict confidentiality agreements, the ethics committee granted a waiver for obtaining individual patient informed consent. However, all patients admitted to the hospital had signed a general consent form permitting the use of their de-identified medical data for retrospective medical research. 2.2 Study subjects and screening process 2.2.1 Study population and source The study population consisted of consecutive patients who presented to the hospital’s Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Vascular Surgery, and Wound Care Center between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024 for diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) complicated by infection. Potential subjects were initially identified through the hospital’s electronic medical record system using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes for diabetic foot and related complications, supplemented by cross-referencing departmental inpatient and outpatient registries to ensure comprehensive inclusion. 2.2.2 Sample size estimation To ensure adequate statistical power, a formal sample size calculation was performed during the study design phase. Based on preliminary literature review and pilot data from our center, we assumed a 6-month ulcer non-healing rate of approximately 40% in patients with moderate infection (Grade 3). To detect a clinically meaningful absolute difference of at least 15% in healing rates between different infection grades (e.g., Grade 2 vs. Grade 4) with a two-sided significance level ( α ) of 0.05 and a power (1-β) of 80%, the formula for comparing two proportions was used. The calculation indicated a requirement of at least 70–90 patients per major comparison group. Considering the planned division into four subgroups and subsequent multivariate analyses, to avoid underpowered analyses, the total sample size target was set at 300 patients. This number was deemed sufficient not only for the primary analyses but also for the planned subgroup analyses and predictive model development. 2.2.3 Inclusion and exclusion criteria Explicit, operational inclusion and exclusion criteria were established. All initially screened medical records were independently reviewed by two researchers. Inclusion
